💓Atrial Fibrillation & PSVT (Supraventricular Tachyarrhythmias)10 items▾

Atrial fibrillation vs PSVT
FeatureAtrial FibrillationPSVTAnswer
Classic vignetteOlder patient, palpitations/dyspnea/fatigue or an embolic event; pulse irregularly irregularSudden-onset, sudden-terminating rapid palpitations in an otherwise stable patient
ECG hallmarkNo consistent P waves + irregularly irregular R-R intervalsRegular narrow-complex tachycardia; P waves may be buried in the QRS
Diagnostic/gold-standard test12-lead ECG; TEE before early cardioversion to exclude LA thrombusECG during the tachycardia; EP study if the mechanism/ablation must be defined
FIRST-LINERate control: beta blocker, diltiazem/verapamil, or digoxinVagal maneuver → adenosine 6 mg rapid IV
ALTRhythm control/cardioversion if symptomatic despite rate controlAdenosine 12 mg if no response; beta blocker or non-dihydropyridine CCB in selected patients
LIFE-SAVINGHemodynamic instability → immediate synchronized cardioversionHypotension/ischemia/pulmonary edema/altered sensorium → synchronized cardioversion
🧠 Memory toolCHA₂DS₂-VASc stroke-risk score in AF
CCongestive heart failure — 1
HHypertension — 1
A₂Age ≥75 — 2
DDiabetes mellitus — 1
S₂Prior Stroke/TIA — 2
VVascular disease — 1
AAge 65–74 — 1
ScSex category: female — 1
The two subscript-2 letters (age ≥75, prior stroke/TIA) are the only 2-point items.
  • ✎Anticoagulate once CHA₂DS₂-VASc is ≥; consider anticoagulation at a score of .
  • ✎Rate-control target in AF: /min at rest and below /min with mild exertion.
Board trap · DOAC in valvular AFAVOID DOACs in rheumatic mitral stenosis or a mechanical valve — use warfarin instead.
A mechanical prosthetic valve needs lifelong vitamin K antagonist (warfarin) anticoagulation; aspirin is not routinely added unless another indication exists or thromboembolism occurs despite therapeutic anticoagulation.
  • ✎Elective cardioversion generally requires ≥ weeks of therapeutic anticoagulation, or may proceed earlier if excludes an LA thrombus.
Recall
Most-tested complication of AF?
tap to flip
Answer
Ischemic stroke / systemic embolism.
  • ★PSVT sequence: Vagal maneuver → Adenosine 6 mg IV → No response → Adenosine 12 mg → Unstable at any point → cardiovert.
🩺 Think it through
A patient with PSVT becomes hypotensive with altered sensorium while vagal maneuvers are being attempted. What is the next step?
Stop the vagal/diagnostic maneuvers and move straight to synchronized cardioversion — do not keep performing maneuvers in a hemodynamically unstable PSVT patient.
Board trap · Stable vs UNSTABLE tachyarrhythmiaA stable tachyarrhythmia earns rate/rhythm drugs and vagal maneuvers, but an UNSTABLE patient (hypotension, ischemia, pulmonary edema, altered sensorium) skips straight to synchronized cardioversion — do not keep escalating drug doses once instability appears.

⚡VT / VF / Sudden Cardiac Death (incl. Torsades de Pointes)14 items▾

VT vs VF vs torsades de pointes
FeatureVTVFTorsades de pointesAnswer
Classic vignettePrior MI/cardiomyopathy + syncope/palpitations + wide-complex tachycardiaCollapse, no pulseOften a QT-prolonging drug exposure
ECG findingWide QRS tachycardia, usually 100–250/minChaotic electrical activity, no effective QRS/no pulsePolymorphic VT with waxing/waning QRS amplitude around baseline
Stable/initial therapyIV amiodarone, procainamide, or lidocaine—IV magnesium 1–2 g
LIFE-SAVINGUnstable → electrical cardioversion/defibrillationImmediate defibrillation + CPRDegeneration to pulseless VT/VF → immediate defibrillation
Recall
Intermittent cannon a waves in the neck veins during a wide-complex tachycardia → origin?
tap to flip
Answer
Ventricular — AV dissociation makes the right atrium contract against a closed tricuspid valve.
Recall
Chronic prevention in high-risk VT/VF survivors?
tap to flip
Answer
Usually an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD).
Board trap · Post-MI ectopyAVOID antiarrhythmic drugs used purely to suppress asymptomatic ventricular ectopy after MI.
Board trap · QT-prolonging drug in torsadesAVOID any QT-prolonging drug in a patient with torsades — it perpetuates the arrhythmia.
Recall
Torsades — alternatives (ALT) to IV magnesium?
tap to flip
Answer
Overdrive pacing; isoproterenol selected for bradycardia-dependent torsades.
  • ✎Torsades de pointes initial therapy: IV g.
  • ★Pause-dependent onset of torsades: premature ventricular beat → pause → sinus beat with a longer QT → its T wave is interrupted by a PVC, which becomes the first beat of the polymorphic VT.
Congenital long QT syndrome — trigger by genotype
GenotypeTypical triggerAnswer
LQTS-1Exertion, particularly swimming
LQTS-2Sudden auditory stimuli or emotional upset
LQTS-3Sudden death tends to occur during sleep
Recall
Short QT syndrome — channel defect and QTc?
tap to flip
Answer
Gain of function of the repolarizing potassium channel (IKr) or reduced inward depolarizing currents → shorter action potential.
QTc <0.36 s, usually <0.3 s.
  • ★Do not delay definitive therapy for further testing in an unstable wide-complex tachycardia — the ECG/monitor tracing is sufficient to act on.
Recall
Most-tested complication of VT/VF?
tap to flip
Answer
Sudden cardiac death.
Board trap · Synchronized vs unsynchronized shockUnstable VT that still has a pulse = synchronized cardioversion.
Pulseless VT/VF = immediate unsynchronized defibrillation plus CPR.
🧠 Memory toolWhich shock for which ventricular rhythm
PulseUnstable VT with a pulse → SYNCHRONIZED cardioversion
No pulsePulseless VT/VF → UNSYNCHRONIZED defibrillation + CPR, immediately
Contrast pair: a pulse to sync with → synchronize; no pulse → defibrillate.

🐢Bradyarrhythmias / AV Block / Sick Sinus Syndrome11 items▾

Bradyarrhythmias — rapid review
Rapid-review targetBoard answerAnswer
Classic vignetteFatigue, dizziness, presyncope/syncope with a slow pulse
Sinus bradycardiaSinus rhythm <60/min
First-degree AV blockPR interval >0.20 s, every P wave followed by a QRS
Sick sinus clueSinus bradycardia/pauses, sometimes alternating with atrial fibrillation/flutter
Gold-standard testECG; Holter, loop recorder, or implanted monitor when symptoms are intermittent. Match the monitor to symptom frequency: a 24-hour Holter is unlikely to capture symptoms that come only once or twice a week → external event recorder; an implantable loop recorder suits much less frequent unexplained events
FIRST-LINECorrect the reversible cause (beta blocker/CCB/digoxin effect, hypothyroidism, metabolic problem)
ALT/definitivePermanent pacemaker for symptomatic intrinsic sinus/AV dysfunction
🧠 Memory toolBradyarrhythmia numbers
60Sinus bradycardia = sinus rhythm <60/min
0.20First-degree AV block = PR >0.20 s (every P still followed by a QRS)
5AF with symptomatic bradycardia/pauses >5 s = pacemaker indication
Number hook: 60 – 0.20 – 5.
Recall
Pacemaker Class I clue?
tap to flip
Answer
Symptomatic sinus bradycardia/pause, or symptomatic chronotropic incompetence.
In acute MI: persistent second-degree AV block in the His-Purkinje system with bilateral bundle branch block is also Class I.
Recall
AV block that worsens with exercise, atropine or isoproterenol → site of block?
tap to flip
Answer
Infranodal. These improve AV-nodal conduction but impair infranodal conduction.
Infranodal block carries a higher risk of progression and is generally an indication for pacing.
  • ✎Atrial fibrillation with symptomatic bradycardia/pauses > s is a pacemaker indication.
Recall
Unstable severe bradycardia / high-grade block → management?
tap to flip
Answer
Atropine and urgent pacing.
Recall
Clinically significant high-grade block during an acute MI — which kind of pacing?
tap to flip
Answer
Temporary pacing while reperfusion and recovery are assessed — the block is often transient, from ischemia of the conduction system.
A permanent pacemaker is reserved for conduction disease that persists after the acute reversible cause is addressed.
Recall
Most-tested complication of bradyarrhythmias?
tap to flip
Answer
Syncope or progression to asystole.
Board trap · Asymptomatic sinus-node dysfunctionAVOID implanting a pacemaker for asymptomatic sinus-node dysfunction alone.
Recall
Sinus bradycardia + first-degree AV block in an asymptomatic endurance athlete → ?
tap to flip
Answer
Common, benign findings of elevated vagal tone — with an otherwise normal examination and ECG, no testing or treatment is needed.
Board trap · Symptoms decide the pacemakerThe same bradyarrhythmia earns different answers by symptom status — symptomatic intrinsic sinus/AV dysfunction gets a permanent pacemaker; the identical finding without symptoms does not.

🚨Shock Syndromes11 items▾

Four shock types
TypeClassic vignetteHemodynamic clueFIRST-LINELIFE-SAVING/definitiveAnswer
HypovolemicHemorrhage, GI loss, dehydration; cold/clammyLow filling pressuresCrystalloid, blood if hemorrhageStop the hemorrhage/source
CardiogenicMI + hypotension + pulmonary congestion/JVD↓ CO, ↑ PCWPDobutamine when inotropy is neededUrgent PCI for an ischemic cause
DistributiveInfection + warm extremities/bounding pulse↓ SVR, often high CO earlyVolume → norepinephrineAntibiotics/source control
ObstructiveHypotension + JVD with tamponade/PE/tension pneumothorax↓ CO despite abnormal filling pressuresCause-specificDrain/decompress/reperfuse
  • ✎Cardiogenic shock after MI: BP < mmHg, PCWP > mmHg, cardiac index < L/min/m² plus hypoperfusion signs.
🧠 Memory toolCardiogenic shock after MI — the three numbers
90BP <90 mmHg
20PCWP >20 mmHg
2.2Cardiac index <2.2 L/min/m²
Plus hypoperfusion signs. Low pressure, high wedge, low index.
  • ✎Harrison shock algorithm: crystalloid bolus commonly mL, reassessing after each bolus.
  • ✎RBC transfusion may be part of shock resuscitation, particularly when Hgb is < g/dL.
  • ✎Oxygen target in shock: SpO₂ %.
Recall
First-line vasopressor for distributive shock? Usual inotrope for cardiogenic shock?
tap to flip
Answer
Norepinephrine for distributive shock; dobutamine for cardiogenic shock.
Recall
Most-tested complication across shock types?
tap to flip
Answer
Multiorgan failure.
Recall
Hypovolemic vs distributive shock — how do they differ at the bedside?
tap to flip
Answer
Hypovolemic: cold extremities, low filling pressures, fluid-responsive.
Distributive: warm extremities, low SVR, needs a vasopressor after initial volume.
Board trap · Blind fluid loading in cardiogenic shockAVOID repeated blind large-volume fluid loading in a pulmonary-congested cardiogenic shock patient.
Board trap · “Give more fluid” is not universal“Give more fluid” is not a universal shock answer — hypovolemic shock wants aggressive crystalloid, but cardiogenic shock with pulmonary congestion needs cautious volume plus an inotrope, not repeated boluses.
Mechanism: cardiogenic shock is LV pump failure (impaired contractility) — the most common cause of shock complicating acute MI; a failing ventricle cannot tolerate added preload, so aggressive fluid worsens pulmonary edema.

🩺Hypertension13 items▾

BP categories
CategoryBP (mmHg)Answer
Normal<120 and <80
Elevated120–129 and <80
Stage 1130–139 OR 80–89
Stage 2≥140 OR ≥90
  • ★Most hypertension is asymptomatic; severe disease may cause headache, visual symptoms, or dizziness.
Recall
Gold-standard test for diagnosing hypertension?
tap to flip
Answer
Harrison assigns no single gold-standard test — diagnosis rests on accurate, repeated BP measurement.
Recall
FIRST-LINE treatment of hypertension?
tap to flip
Answer
Lifestyle modification plus a thiazide-type diuretic, ACE inhibitor/ARB, or calcium-channel blocker, chosen by comorbidity; combine agents if one does not control BP.
Significant albuminuria (e.g. diabetic nephropathy) → ACE inhibitor/ARB preferred in the initial regimen: RAAS blockade lowers intraglomerular pressure and proteinuria, protecting the kidney beyond BP lowering.
Antihypertensives to AVOID
Drug classAVOID inAnswer
ACEi/ARBPregnancy or bilateral renal artery stenosis
Beta blockersUncontrolled asthma / advanced block
Verapamil/diltiazemAdvanced AV block or HFrEF
Recall
Persistent severe-range hypertension in pregnancy — drug of choice?
tap to flip
Answer
Labetalol (first-line); lifestyle measures alone are inadequate.
ACE inhibitors are contraindicated (fetal toxicity); spironolactone is avoided (antiandrogenic effects).
Recall
What defines a hypertensive emergency?
tap to flip
Answer
Acute cardiac, neurologic, or renal decompensation — a severe BP number alone is not sufficient.
Recall
FIRST-LINE IV options in hypertensive emergency?
tap to flip
Answer
Nicardipine, labetalol, nitroprusside, nitroglycerin, or a condition-specific agent.
  • ✎IV nicardipine: start mg/h, titrate by mg/h, max mg/h.
  • ✎IV labetalol: mg over 2 min, then mg every 10 min, max total mg.
Board trap · Abrupt BP normalizationAVOID abrupt normalization of BP in most hypertensive emergencies — Harrison recommends gradual MAP reduction over several hours unless the specific condition dictates otherwise.
Recall
Most-tested complications of hypertension?
tap to flip
Answer
Stroke, coronary artery disease, heart failure.
Board trap · Urgency vs emergencyDecided by target-organ damage, not the BP number.
Urgency: severe asymptomatic elevation without organ injury → oral therapy, gradual control.
Emergency: acute end-organ decompensation → monitored IV therapy.

🏃Stable Coronary Artery Disease / Stable Angina9 items▾

Stable angina — rapid review
Rapid-review targetBoard answerAnswer
Classic vignettePredictable substernal pressure with exertion/emotion, relieved by rest or nitroglycerin
Classic findingExertional ischemia; resting ECG may be normal
First testExercise ECG, if the patient can exercise and the resting ECG is interpretable
Anatomic definitive testCoronary angiography when the anatomy will change the revascularization decision
FIRST-LINERisk-factor reduction + antiplatelet/statin; beta blocker for symptom control
ALTCalcium-channel blocker, long-acting nitrate, or ranolazine
Recall
First test in stable angina — and its two preconditions?
tap to flip
Answer
Exercise ECG — if the patient can exercise and the resting ECG is interpretable.
Board trap · False-negative stress ECGObstructive disease limited to the circumflex artery can give a false-negative exercise ECG — the lateral wall it supplies is poorly represented on the surface 12-lead ECG.
Board trap · Verapamil + beta blockerVerapamil ordinarily should not be combined with a beta blocker — their depressant effects on heart rate and contractility are additive.
  • ★No fixed numeric diagnostic criteria are given for stable angina — it is a clinical, exertional-pattern diagnosis.
Board trap · Stenosis alone is not an indicationAVOID revascularization merely because a stenosis exists, if symptoms or risk do not justify it.
🩺 Think it through
A patient with long-standing predictable exertional angina now reports new pain at rest in a crescendo pattern. How should this be managed?
Emergency escalation: new rest pain, a crescendo pattern, or a biomarker rise → manage as acute coronary syndrome, not stable angina.
Recall
Most-tested complication of stable CAD?
tap to flip
Answer
Acute myocardial infarction.
Board trap · “Stable” until the pattern changes“Stable” angina stops being stable the moment the pattern changes — rest pain, a crescendo pattern, or a positive biomarker mean the vignette is now an ACS, and management shifts from elective testing to an acute workup.

🚑ST-Elevation Myocardial Infarction (STEMI)11 items▾

STEMI — rapid review
Rapid-review targetBoard answerAnswer
Classic vignetteProlonged crushing chest pain + diaphoresis + ST elevation
Harrison ECG criterion>1 mm ST elevation in 2 contiguous limb leads OR ≥2 mm in 2 contiguous precordial leads; a new LBBB also counts
Best initial testImmediate 12-lead ECG
BiomarkerCardiac troponin T/I — preferred marker of myocardial injury
FIRST-LINE drugAspirin 162–325 mg, chewed immediately
Definitive therapyPrimary PCI, preferred
ALTFibrinolysis if PCI is unavailable or FMC-to-PCI delay >120 min, and no contraindication
  • ✎STEMI ECG criterion: > mm ST elevation in 2 contiguous limb leads OR ≥ mm in 2 contiguous precordial leads; a new also counts.
  • ✎Total coronary occlusion without collaterals: damage is reversible up to min; beyond min it is permanent (myocardial necrosis).
Board trap · Waiting for troponinCritical board rule: do not wait for troponin before reperfusion when history + ECG already diagnose STEMI.
  • ✎Fibrinolysis target: door-to-needle < min.
Recall
AVOID fibrinolysis in STEMI when…? (5)
tap to flip
Answer
Prior intracranial bleed, recent major CNS event, aortic dissection, active bleeding, or severe uncontrolled hypertension.
  • ✎Rescue PCI: persistent chest pain or ST elevation > min after fibrinolysis signals failed reperfusion.
Recall
Most-tested complications of STEMI?
tap to flip
Answer
VT/VF, cardiogenic shock, or mechanical rupture.
🧠 Memory toolSTEMI reperfusion clock
30Door-to-needle <30 min for fibrinolysis
90Pain/ST elevation persisting >90 min after fibrinolysis = failed reperfusion → rescue PCI
120FMC-to-PCI ≤120 min → primary PCI; delay >120 min (or PCI unavailable) → fibrinolysis
Number hook: 30 – 90 – 120.
  • ★STEMI sequence: History + ECG diagnose STEMI → Aspirin 162–325 mg chewed → FMC-to-PCI ≤120 min → Primary PCI → Unavailable/>120 min → Fibrinolysis (door-to-needle <30 min) → Failed reperfusion (pain/ST elevation >90 min) → Rescue PCI.
Board trap · Fibrinolysis is STEMI-onlyFibrinolysis is a STEMI-only tool — AVOID fibrinolytic therapy in NSTEMI, which has no occlusive thrombus pattern to lyse.

💔NSTEMI / Unstable Angina6 items▾

NSTEMI / unstable angina — rapid review
Rapid-review targetBoard answerAnswer
Classic vignetteRest angina, new severe angina, or rapidly worsening chronic angina
NSTEMI discriminatorElevated cardiac troponin
UA discriminatorACS symptoms without biomarker evidence of myocardial necrosis
ECGST depression and/or T-wave inversion may occur
Diagnostic testSerial ECG + serial troponins
FIRST-LINEAspirin 325 mg initially → 75–100 mg/day, plus a P2Y12 inhibitor and anticoagulation as appropriate
ALTFondaparinux or bivalirudin in appropriate situations
  • ✎NSTEMI/UA: aspirin mg initially → mg/day, plus a P2Y12 inhibitor and anticoagulation as appropriate.
Board trap · Fibrinolysis in NSTEMI/UAAVOID fibrinolytic therapy in NSTEMI/unstable angina.
Recall
NSTEMI/UA with high-risk features or refractory ischemia → ?
tap to flip
Answer
LIFE-SAVING/high-risk: early invasive coronary angiography and revascularization.
Recall
Most-tested complication of NSTEMI/UA?
tap to flip
Answer
Progression to MI or recurrent ischemia.
Recall
NSTEMI vs unstable angina — what separates them, and what do both get?
tap to flip
Answer
NSTEMI: ACS with an elevated troponin (myocardial necrosis has occurred).
UA: ACS symptoms with a normal troponin (ischemia without necrosis).
Both: antiplatelet/anticoagulant therapy and risk-stratified invasive angiography — never fibrinolysis.

🫀Heart Failure / Ventricular Dysfunction11 items▾

Heart failure — rapid review
Rapid-review targetBoard answerAnswer
Classic vignette openerDyspnea + orthopnea/PND + edema + JVD
HFrEF clueS3 (protodiastolic gallop, early diastole — most common with volume overload plus tachycardia/tachypnea; often signifies severe hemodynamic compromise), volume overload, reduced systolic function
HFpEF clueS4 (atrial-contraction gallop), preserved systolic EF with impaired filling
First imaging testEchocardiography with Doppler
Lab discriminatorBNP/NT-proBNP ↑ favors cardiac rather than pulmonary dyspnea
MRA cutoffConsider in class II–IV HF with LVEF <35%
ICD cutoffChronic class II–III HF with LVEF <35%
🧠 Memory toolLVEF <35% — what it unlocks
MRAConsider in class II–IV HF with LVEF <35%
ICDChronic class II–III HF with LVEF <35%
Same EF cutoff (35%); the NYHA range differs — MRA II–IV, ICD II–III.
Recall
FIRST-LINE therapy for chronic HFrEF?
tap to flip
Answer
ACE inhibitor + evidence-based beta blocker; add a diuretic for congestion.
Recall
Add-on options in chronic HFrEF?
tap to flip
Answer
ARB, hydralazine/nitrate combination, MRA, digoxin, ivabradine, or a device (ICD/CRT) per indication.
Recall
Most-tested complication of heart failure?
tap to flip
Answer
Acute pulmonary edema or sudden cardiac death.
Recall
Unilateral pleural effusion in heart failure — which side is more frequent?
tap to flip
Answer
The right pleural space (HF effusions are often bilateral).
Recall
Cheyne-Stokes respiration in a patient with worsening heart failure → first step?
tap to flip
Answer
Optimize heart-failure therapy. Crescendo-decrescendo breathing with central apneas (no snoring) is central sleep apnea driven by circulatory delay and hypocapnia; it typically improves as volume status and cardiac function improve.
Board trap · ACEi/ARB and MRA — lab limitsAVOID an ACE inhibitor/ARB when K⁺ >5.5, creatinine >3 mg/dL, bilateral renal artery stenosis, or pregnancy.
AVOID an MRA when K⁺ >5.0 or creatinine >2.5 mg/dL.
Board trap · Beta blocker timing in HFAVOID starting a beta blocker in unstable/decompensated HF, symptomatic bradycardia, or advanced heart block — start it only once the patient is euvolemic and stable.
Once there, add a mortality-reducing beta blocker such as carvedilol. Ivabradine is reserved for persistent sinus tachycardia despite a maximally tolerated beta blocker; CRT/ICD come after medical therapy is optimized.
Acute decompensated HF — hemodynamic-profile-guided therapy
Hemodynamic profileManagementAnswer
Warm + wetIV loop diuretic + vasodilator
Cold + wetVasodilator + inotropic agent as needed
Cold + dryIf PCWP <12 mmHg, cautious volume trial
Warm + drySearch for a noncongestive cause of symptoms
  • ✎Hospitalized volume-overloaded HF patient: IV loop diuretic, targeting a weight loss of kg/day.

🦠Infective Endocarditis13 items▾

Infective endocarditis — rapid review
Rapid-review targetBoard answerAnswer
Classic vignette openerFever + new/changing murmur ± embolic/immunologic manifestations
Classic findingPersistent bacteremia + valvular vegetation
Diagnostic criteriaModified Duke Criteria

Minor fever cutoff≥38.0°C

22 major
1 + 31 major + 3 minor

Number hook: 2 – 1+3 – 5. Any one combination = definite IE.
Recall
Duke MAJOR blood-culture criterion?
tap to flip
Answer
A typical organism recovered from 2 separate cultures, persistently compatible cultures, or a Coxiella burnetii criterion.
Recall
Duke MAJOR echo/endocardial criterion?
tap to flip
Answer
Vegetation, abscess, prosthetic dehiscence, or new regurgitation.

Recall
FIRST-LINE management of infective endocarditis?
tap to flip
Answer
Obtain blood cultures first, then start prolonged bactericidal IV antibiotics tailored to the organism.

tap to flip
Answer
Prosthetic valve (bioprosthetic included): highest-risk category → prophylaxis for life, however old or well-functioning the valve.
Prosthetic material closing a septal defect: first 6 months only (until endothelialization), unless a residual defect persists.

Board trap · Cultures before antibioticsStable subacute IE: AVOID starting antibiotics before adequate blood cultures are drawn — wait for the cultures.
Acute or hemodynamically unstable IE: draw 3 sets of cultures fast and start antibiotics without delay.
  • ✎Persistent fever after days of appropriate IE therapy → search for a paravalvular or extracardiac .
  • ✎A negative TEE despite high clinical suspicion of IE should be repeated in days.
Recall
IE with valve dysfunction + pulmonary edema or cardiogenic shock → ?
tap to flip
Answer
LIFE-SAVING: same-day/emergent surgery.
Recall
Most-tested complication of infective endocarditis?
tap to flip
Answer
Acute valvular heart failure.

💉Urticaria and Anaphylaxis21 items▾

Urticaria vs anaphylaxis
FeatureUrticariaAnaphylaxisAnswer
Lesion/onsetTransient pruritic wheal, pale/blanched centerSeconds to minutes after allergen exposure: pruritus/urticaria + angioedema + wheeze/stridor ± hypotension/GI symptoms

  • ★Anaphylaxis sequence: Recognize urticaria/angioedema + wheeze/stridor ± hypotension → IM epinephrine 0.3–0.5 mg stat → repeat q5–20 min if persistent → supportive: O2, IV fluids, positioning, bronchodilator/antihistamine adjuncts → observe for biphasic reaction.

IM epinephrine 0.3–0.5 mg (1 mg/mL) immediately, repeated every 5–20 min if the severe reaction persists. Antihistamines and glucocorticoids are adjuncts only; then supportive care and observation for a biphasic reaction.

A physical urticaria: a linear wheal with surrounding erythema after brisk stroking of the skin.

  • ✎Hematochezia can occur with rapid UGIB when blood loss exceeds mL.

Clean ulcer base = low rebleeding risk → no endoscopic hemostasis needed.

tap to flip

Only a temporary bridge when bleeding is uncontrolled.

tap to flip

Painless → diverticular or angiodysplastic bleeding.

🩺 Think it through
A patient passes large amounts of bright red blood per rectum and is hemodynamically unstable. What is done, and which scope comes first?
Unstable hematochezia may represent rapid UGIB: resuscitate, then EGD first to exclude a brisk upper source before pursuing lower-source control. Do not automatically assume hematochezia = lower source.

tap to flip

Cause-specific therapy plus treatment of each complication.

tap to flip

New GI bleeding, infection, encephalopathy, AKI, or rapidly worsening ascites.

tap to flip

↑ Intrahepatic resistance (cirrhosis and regenerative nodules) plus ↑ splanchnic blood flow (splanchnic vasodilation).

tap to flip

Gold standard: HVPG measurement.
Changes bleeding-prevention management: EGD for varices.

tap to flip

High-risk varices: nonselective beta blocker and/or EVL.
Refractory portal-hypertensive complications: TIPS is the alternative.
Recall

tap to flip
Answer
Creates a direct intrahepatic portosystemic pathway that decompresses portal hypertension.
The diverted portal blood bypasses hepatic detoxification → ammonia and other neurotoxins reach the systemic circulation → ↑ risk of hepatic encephalopathy.

tap to flip

Vasoactive therapy plus urgent EVL.

Portal hypertension → splenomegaly with hypersplenism → ↓ platelets and ↓ white cells; the same portal hypertension explains the varices and ascites.

In patients at high risk for renal/hepatic deterioration.

Investigate for secondary peritonitis.
Multiple organisms with an elevated PMN count point to a perforated viscus or another intra-abdominal source.

Recall

tap to flip
Answer
Severe postpartum hemorrhage → failure to lactate + amenorrhea → fatigue, hypotension, cold intolerance.

tap to flip

8-AM cortisol, TSH + free T4, IGF-1, prolactin, and gonadal-axis evaluation.

tap to flip
Answer

A woman who had severe postpartum hemorrhage cannot lactate, has amenorrhea, fatigue, hypotension and cold intolerance; free T4 is low with an inappropriately normal TSH. Which hormone is replaced first?
Sheehan syndrome (hypopituitarism). Start glucocorticoid first, then levothyroxine — thyroid hormone first can unmask/worsen adrenal insufficiency; then replace every deficient target hormone.

Total-body potassium is depleted.

tap to flip

tap to flip
Answer
Severe hyperglycemia/hyperosmolality with minimal ketogenesis.

DKAKetones strongly positive, anion gap ↑, bicarbonate <15 mEq/L, pH 6.8–7.3, glucose 250–600 mg/dL
HHSOsmolality 330–380 mOsm/kg, glucose 600–1200 mg/dL, pH >7.3, ketones absent/minimal

🩺 Think it through
A type 1 diabetic who missed insulin presents with vomiting, abdominal pain, Kussmaul respirations and fruity breath. Serum K⁺ is below 3.3 mEq/L. Is insulin started now?
No — HOLD insulin and replace potassium first (K⁺ <3.3 mEq/L is the critical contraindication); start 0.9% normal saline. Hypokalemia during treatment is the most-tested complication.

Answer
Ketoconazole, metyrapone, or mitotane.
  • ★Most-tested complication of Cushing syndrome: diabetes/HTN/osteoporosis, with major cardiovascular and infectious morbidity.
  • ★Cushing work-up sequence: Screen (UFC / late-night salivary cortisol / 1-mg dexamethasone) → Confirm hypercortisolism → Measure ACTH → Localize (imaging ± petrosal sinus sampling).
🧠 Memory toolCushing work-up order
SScreen — UFC / late-night salivary cortisol / 1-mg dexamethasone
CConfirm hypercortisolism
AACTH — adrenal vs pituitary/ectopic
LLocalize — imaging ± petrosal sinus sampling
"SCAL" before the scalpel: biochemistry first, imaging last.
Board trap · Never stop chronic steroids abruptlyNever abruptly stop chronic exogenous glucocorticoids — this precipitates adrenal crisis from HPA-axis suppression.
Board trap · Imaging before biochemistryTempting: imaging the adrenals or pituitary straight away.
Right: do not image before biochemically proving hypercortisolism.
Why: premature imaging can turn up an incidental adrenal lesion and lead to inappropriate or unnecessary surgery — localization studies only find the source after the diagnosis is established.

🧂Primary Hyperaldosteronism (Conn Syndrome)13 items▾

Recall
Primary hyperaldosteronism — classic vignette opener?
tap to flip
Answer
Resistant hypertension + hypokalemia + metabolic alkalosis + no edema.
Recall
Primary aldosteronism — screening test?
tap to flip
Answer
Plasma aldosterone + plasma renin activity (aldosterone-renin ratio).
Screen when hypertension comes with: resistance to treatment, hypokalemia, an adrenal mass, or young onset — aldosterone and renin are measured simultaneously.
  • ✎Screening clue for primary aldosteronism: aldosterone-renin ratio > (Harrison's specified units) plus aldosterone > pmol/L.
Board trap · ARR while still hypokalemicTempting: accepting a negative aldosterone-renin ratio drawn while potassium is low.
Right: normalize potassium before testing — hypokalemia can lower aldosterone and give a false-negative screen.
  • ✎Confirmatory test: L IV normal saline over h; positive = aldosterone fails to suppress below ng/dL (140 pmol/L).
Recall
Hypertension + hypokalemia with BOTH renin and aldosterone suppressed → diagnosis and mechanism?
tap to flip
Answer
Apparent mineralocorticoid excess — loss or inhibition of 11β-HSD2 lets cortisol activate mineralocorticoid receptors.
(Primary aldosteronism has suppressed renin but high aldosterone.)
Recall
Primary aldosteronism — localization?
tap to flip
Answer
High-resolution adrenal CT; adrenal-vein sampling if unilateral secretion remains uncertain.
In older patients a unilateral nodule on CT may be an incidental nonfunctioning adenoma, so adrenal-vein sampling is often used in surgical candidates to prove lateralization.
Recall
FIRST-LINE: unilateral adenoma vs bilateral hyperplasia?
tap to flip
Answer
Unilateral adenoma: adrenalectomy.
Bilateral hyperplasia: spironolactone.
  • ✎Bilateral adrenal hyperplasia: spironolactone mg BID; preferred alternative eplerenone mg BID; is another option.
  • ★EMERGENCY: severe hypokalemia/arrhythmia or hypertensive crisis → stabilize electrolytes/BP. Most-tested complication: hypokalemic arrhythmia / cardiovascular disease.
Board trap · No adrenalectomy for bilateral hyperplasiaAVOID adrenalectomy for bilateral adrenal hyperplasia — bilateral disease is managed medically (mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist).
Surgery is reserved for a unilateral aldosterone-producing adenoma.
🧠 Memory toolConn syndrome: one side vs two sides
UnilateralAdenoma → adrenalectomy (cut)
BilateralHyperplasia → spironolactone 25–100 mg BID (block)
One gland = knife; two glands = pills.
🩺 Think it through
A patient with resistant hypertension, hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis without edema has a positive screen; after 2 L IV saline over 4 h aldosterone remains above 5 ng/dL. Adrenal CT shows bilateral hyperplasia. Treatment?
Primary aldosteronism from bilateral hyperplasia → spironolactone 25–100 mg BID (eplerenone 25–50 mg BID as alternative). AVOID adrenalectomy — surgery is only for a unilateral adenoma.

🛡️Adrenal Insufficiency: Addison Disease & Adrenal Crisis14 items▾

Adrenal insufficiency — rapid-review targets
Rapid-review targetBoard answerAnswer
Classic vignette openerWeight loss + fatigue + orthostatic hypotension + salt craving + GI symptoms
Classic findingCutaneous/mucosal hyperpigmentation + hyponatremia ↓ + hyperkalemia ↑
Best test250-µg cosyntropin stimulation test
Normal responseCortisol should exceed 18 µg/dL at 30–60 min
Primary diseaseACTH high
Secondary diseaseACTH low/inappropriately normal; K⁺ generally not elevated
FIRST-LINEHydrocortisone 15–25 mg/day
MineralocorticoidFludrocortisone 0.05–0.1 mg/day
AVOIDFailure to stress-dose during major illness
LIFE-SAVING emergencyAdrenal crisis → high-dose IV hydrocortisone + normal saline
Most-tested complicationAdrenal crisis
  • ✎Cosyntropin stimulation test: µg; normal cortisol exceeds µg/dL at min.
  • ✎Chronic replacement in Addison disease: hydrocortisone mg/day and fludrocortisone mg/day.
Recall
Primary vs secondary adrenal insufficiency — ACTH and K⁺?
tap to flip
Answer
Primary: ACTH high, K⁺ elevated.
Secondary: ACTH low/inappropriately normal, K⁺ generally normal.
Why: primary disease also causes mineralocorticoid (aldosterone) deficiency → sodium loss, hyperkalemia and ↑ renin; mineralocorticoid secretion is generally preserved in secondary disease.
Recall
Why is hyperpigmentation seen in primary but not secondary adrenal insufficiency?
tap to flip
Answer
Primary failure removes cortisol feedback → high ACTH and other POMC-derived peptides that stimulate pigmentation.
Secondary disease has deficient ACTH/POMC signaling → no hyperpigmentation.
Recall
Adrenal crisis — classic vignette opener?
tap to flip
Answer
Addison/steroid-dependent patient with infection, surgery, or vomiting → profound hypotension + abdominal symptoms ± Na⁺ ↓, K⁺ ↑, glucose ↓.
  • ★No single pathognomonic finding in adrenal crisis — shock in known/suspected adrenal insufficiency is itself the board trigger.
  • ✎Adrenal crisis, FIRST-LINE / LIFE-SAVING: hydrocortisone mg IV. Alternative regimen: mg/h continuous IV, or 100-mg bolus IV times daily.
Recall
Adrenal crisis — required support besides hydrocortisone?
tap to flip
Answer
Normal saline ± glucose correction, plus treatment of the precipitant.
  • ★Adrenal crisis diagnostic test: draw cortisol/ACTH if immediately feasible — but never delay treatment for it.
  • ★EMERGENCY — most-tested complication of adrenal crisis: refractory shock / death.
Board trap · Do not wait for the cosyntropin testNever wait for cosyntropin testing before giving steroids in suspected adrenal crisis — treat empirically with IV hydrocortisone + saline immediately; the test can follow.
🧠 Memory toolAdrenal insufficiency number hook
250µg cosyntropin for the stimulation test
18µg/dL — cortisol should exceed this at 30–60 min
15–25mg/day hydrocortisone maintenance
0.05–0.1mg/day fludrocortisone
100mg IV hydrocortisone in crisis
Test 250 → pass 18 → maintain 15–25 → crisis 100.
🩺 Think it through
A steroid-dependent patient develops vomiting after surgery and arrives in profound hypotension with low sodium, high potassium and low glucose. Should cosyntropin testing be done before treatment?
No. Adrenal crisis → hydrocortisone 100 mg IV + normal saline immediately (± glucose correction, treat the precipitant). Draw cortisol/ACTH only if immediately feasible; the test can follow.

⚡Pheochromocytoma10 items▾

🧠 Memory toolPheochromocytoma classic triad
HHeadache — episodic
PPalpitations
DDiaphoresis — profuse
In a young/middle-aged hypertensive patient.
Recall
Young/middle-aged hypertensive with episodic headache + palpitations + profuse diaphoresis → diagnosis?
tap to flip
Answer
Pheochromocytoma (the classic triad).
Recall
Pheochromocytoma — first biochemical test?
tap to flip
Answer
Plasma metanephrines, or 24-h urinary catecholamine metabolites/metanephrines.
Board trap · Imaging before biochemistryTempting: CT/MRI as the first step.
Right: localize with CT or MRI only AFTER biochemical evidence is obtained — imaging never precedes the biochemical work-up.
  • ★Harrison's Manual does not designate one single "gold standard" test for pheochromocytoma; biochemical confirmation precedes imaging.
Recall
Pheochromocytoma — definitive management?
tap to flip
Answer
Surgical management of functional adrenal masses after appropriate evaluation.
Board trap · Alpha-blockade before beta-blockadePreoperative preparation of a confirmed pheochromocytoma: alpha-adrenergic blockade with salt and volume repletion first → beta-blocker added later only if needed for tachycardia.
Tempting: a beta-blocker first to slow the heart.
Right: AVOID — beta-blockade before alpha-blockade leaves unopposed alpha-mediated vasoconstriction and can trigger severe hypertension.
Recall
Pheochromocytoma — emergency and most-tested complication?
tap to flip
Answer
EMERGENCY: catecholamine crisis/hypertensive emergency → monitored emergency BP management.
Most-tested complication: hypertensive crisis / stroke or arrhythmia.
  • ★Pheochromocytoma sequence: Episodic headache + palpitations + diaphoresis → Plasma/urine metanephrines → CT/MRI localization → Surgical management.
Board trap · Never needle a pheochromocytomaFine-needle aspiration is absolutely contraindicated if pheochromocytoma is suspected — needling a catecholamine-secreting tumor can precipitate a hypertensive crisis.

🦴Hyperparathyroidism & Hypercalcemic Crisis19 items▾

🧠 Memory toolHypercalcemia / hyperparathyroidism presentation
StonesNephrolithiasis
BonesOsteoporosis
GroansConstipation, weakness
Psychiatric overtonesNeuropsychiatric symptoms
"Stones, bones, groans, psychiatric overtones."
Recall
Primary hyperparathyroidism — classic biochemical finding?
tap to flip
Answer
Hypercalcemia ↑ + inappropriately elevated/nonsuppressed PTH.
  • ✎Reference serum calcium (Harrison's figure): mg/dL.
Albumin-corrected calcium
Corrected Ca = measured Ca + 0.8 mg/dL × (4.1 − albumin in g/dL)
Add 0.8 mg/dL to measured calcium per 1 g/dL that albumin is below 4.1 g/dL.
Measured Ca 8.0 mg/dL, albumin 2.1 g/dL: 4.1 − 2.1 = 2.0; 2.0 × 0.8 = 1.6; corrected Ca = 8.0 + 1.6 = 9.6 mg/dL.
Recall
Key mimic of primary hyperparathyroidism and the distinguishing test?
tap to flip
Answer
Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia (FHH) — PTH is often nonsuppressed, but urinary calcium is low.
Recall
Hyperparathyroidism — FIRST-LINE definitive therapy when indicated?
tap to flip
Answer
Parathyroidectomy.
  • ✎Parathyroidectomy indications: age <, nephrolithiasis, CrCl < mL/min, T-score <, or serum Ca >1 mg/dL above normal.
🧠 Memory toolParathyroidectomy indications
Age<50
StonesNephrolithiasis
KidneyCrCl <60 mL/min
BoneT-score <−2.5
CalciumSerum Ca >1 mg/dL above normal
Number hook: 50 – 60 – 2.5 – 1.
  • ★EMERGENCY: severe symptomatic hypercalcemia → saline-based hypercalcemia treatment. Most-tested complication of hyperparathyroidism: nephrolithiasis.
Board trap · Never operate for FHHParathyroid surgery is contraindicated in familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia.
The low urinary calcium (not the PTH level) is what separates FHH from primary hyperparathyroidism.
Recall
Severe hypercalcemia / hypercalcemic crisis — classic vignette opener?
tap to flip
Answer
Cancer or hyperparathyroidism + dehydration + confusion + constipation/polyuria.
  • ✎Severe hypercalcemia cutoff: Ca > mg/dL.
  • ★EMERGENCY clue: very high calcium levels can progress to coma/cardiac arrest — the most-tested complication of hypercalcemic crisis.
Recall
Hypercalcemia — first diagnostic discriminator?
tap to flip
Answer
PTH level → separates PTH-dependent from PTH-independent hypercalcemia.
Intact PTH is elevated or inappropriately normal in most parathyroid-mediated hypercalcemia; suppressed in most malignancy-related and other non-parathyroid causes.
Recall
Humoral hypercalcemia of malignancy — mediator, and what happens to intact PTH?
tap to flip
Answer
Usually mediated by PTHrP; the resulting hypercalcemia suppresses endogenous intact PTH.
Recall
Hypercalcemic crisis — FIRST-LINE emergency therapy and preferred sustained therapy?
tap to flip
Answer
FIRST-LINE: IV normal saline hydration.
Sustained: IV bisphosphonate (pamidronate/zoledronate).
Recall
Hypercalcemic crisis — rapid alternative/add-on and special rescue?
tap to flip
Answer
Calcitonin — rapid onset, but tachyphylaxis develops.
Special rescue: dialysis in extreme circumstances/renal failure.
  • ✎Calcitonin in hypercalcemia: rapid onset, but tachyphylaxis develops after days.
Board trap · Diuresis before rehydrationAVOID forced diuresis before adequate volume repletion — give IV normal saline first; diuretics before rehydration worsen volume depletion.

🤏Hypoparathyroidism / Hypocalcemia11 items▾

Recall
Hypoparathyroidism/hypocalcemia — classic vignette opener?
tap to flip
Answer
After thyroid/neck surgery → perioral tingling + hand spasm/tetany.
🧠 Memory toolClassic findings of hypocalcemia
CChvostek sign
TTrousseau sign
QTProlonged QT
Two signs + one ECG finding, classically after thyroid/neck surgery.
Recall
Hypoparathyroidism — biochemical pattern?
tap to flip
Answer
Calcium ↓ + phosphate ↑ + PTH low/inappropriately normal.
Recall
Hypocalcemia — which other electrolyte must be measured, and why?
tap to flip
Answer
Magnesium — severe hypomagnesemia can prevent calcium correction.
  • ★Gold-standard concept: serum/ionized Ca + PTH + Mg/phosphate together define the mechanism of hypocalcemia.
  • ✎Chronic hypoparathyroidism, FIRST-LINE: calcium g/day + calcitriol µg/day.
  • ✎LIFE-SAVING for symptomatic hypocalcemia: calcium gluconate g IV over min; preferred add-on: correct any deficiency.
  • ★EMERGENCY — most-tested complication of hypocalcemia: tetany / laryngospasm or seizure.
Board trap · Calcium fails without magnesiumTempting: re-dosing calcium again and again.
Right: repeated calcium alone fails if severe hypomagnesemia persists — magnesium must be corrected for calcium to normalize; do not keep re-dosing calcium without checking Mg.
Hypoparathyroidism vs primary hyperparathyroidism
DisorderCalciumPhosphatePTHAnswer
Hypoparathyroidism↓↑Low/inappropriate (inappropriately normal)
Primary hyperparathyroidism↑—Inappropriately high/nonsuppressed
🩺 Think it through
One day after thyroidectomy a patient has perioral tingling, hand spasm and a prolonged QT; symptoms persist despite repeated IV calcium. What was missed?
Check and correct magnesium — severe hypomagnesemia prevents calcium correction. Continue calcium gluconate 1–2 g IV over 10–20 min for symptoms.

Anemia — rapid-review targets
Rapid-review targetBoard answerAnswer
Classic vignette openerPallor + fatigue + exertional dyspnea + tachycardia ± bleeding history
Male cutoffHb <13 g/dL or Hct <39%
Female cutoffHb <12 g/dL or Hct <37%

RI <2–2.5%Inadequate marrow production
RI >2.5%Hemolysis or blood loss

Recall
Anemia work-up: which test do you check FIRST, and why?
tap to flip
Answer
Reticulocyte index (RI) first — it tells you whether the marrow is responding before you build the rest of the differential.
MCV then narrows the cause further.
🧠 Memory toolThe RI dividing line (contrast pair)
RI <2–2.5%Underproduction — inadequate marrow production
RI >2.5%Hemolysis or blood loss — marrow is responding
Read the RI before the MCV.
Board trap · MCV before RITempting: jumping straight to a microcytic/macrocytic cause.
Right: check the RI first — RI <2–2.5% points to underproduction, RI >2.5% points to hemolysis or blood loss. Picking a microcytic/macrocytic cause before checking the RI skips the step the exam is actually testing.
  • ✎Anemia cut-offs — male: Hb < g/dL or Hct <%; female: Hb < g/dL or Hct <37%.
  • ✎MCV branch (Harrison's general algorithm): microcytic < fL; macrocytic > fL.

Hb/Hct immediately after an acute hemorrhage?
tap to flip
Answer
Can be deceptively normal at first — the values fall only after hemodilution equilibrates.
Expected response to packed RBC transfusion
1 unit packed RBCs → Hb ↑ ≈ 1 g/dL and Hct ↑ 3–4%
Applies once bleeding has stopped.
2 units → Hb ↑ ≈ 2 × 1 = 2 g/dL; Hct ↑ ≈ 2 × (3–4) = 6–8%
Recall
Gold-standard test for anemia?
tap to flip
Answer
None for anemia as a syndrome — the etiology requires cause-specific testing.
Recall
Anemia with acute severe blood loss/ischemia → LIFE-SAVING step? Most-tested complication?
tap to flip
Answer
Hemorrhage control + packed RBC transfusion as indicated.
Complication: tissue hypoxia / myocardial ischemia.

🧲Microcytic/Normocytic Anemias: Iron Deficiency vs. Anemia of Inflammation14 items▾

Iron-deficiency anemia vs. anemia of inflammation/chronic disease
FeatureIron-deficiency anemiaAnemia of inflammation/chronic diseaseAnswer
Classic vignetteChronic blood loss → fatigue/pallor + microcytic hypochromic anemia; adult male/postmenopausal woman should trigger a search for occult GI bleedingChronic infection, inflammatory disease, malignancy, or systemic illness + mild normocytic/microcytic anemia
Serum iron<30 µg/dL<50 µg/dL
TIBC>360 µg/dL<300 µg/dL
Transferrin saturation<10%10–20%
Ferritin<15 µg/L30–200 µg/L (preserved/increased)
Gold-standard testIron studies — marrow iron rarely needed when routine tests are diagnosticNo single confirmatory test — clinical context + iron-study pattern
FIRST-LINEOral iron (regimen: ferrous sulfate 300 mg PO TID) + identify/stop the bleeding sourceTreat the underlying disease
ALTParenteral iron when oral iron cannot be used/absorbedErythropoietin in appropriate renal/selected hypoproliferative disease
AVOIDGiving iron indefinitely without investigating unexplained blood lossRoutine iron supplementation / assuming low serum iron automatically means iron deficiency when true deficiency has not been demonstrated
🧠 Memory toolIron studies — which way do TIBC and ferritin point?
IDAIron ↓ + TIBC HIGH + ferritin LOW
AIIron ↓ + TIBC LOW + ferritin preserved/HIGH
Low iron is shared by both — the TIBC and ferritin direction separates them.
Board trap · Low iron ≠ iron deficiencyTempting: low serum iron → call it iron deficiency.
Right: low iron + HIGH TIBC + LOW ferritin = iron-deficiency anemia; low iron + LOW TIBC + preserved/HIGH ferritin = anemia of inflammation. The TIBC and ferritin direction, not the low iron alone, separates the two.
  • ✎Iron-deficiency anemia: ferritin < µg/L, TIBC > µg/dL, transferrin saturation <%.
  • ✎Anemia of inflammation: ferritin µg/L (preserved/increased), TIBC < µg/dL, saturation %.
  • ✎Serum iron: iron-deficiency anemia < µg/dL; anemia of inflammation < µg/dL.
Recall
Iron deficiency: why do the red cells end up small and pale?
tap to flip
Answer
Stores are exhausted → serum iron falls, TIBC rises, transferrin saturation declines → hemoglobin synthesis is impaired → microcytic, hypochromic cells.
Recall
Anemia of inflammation can be microcytic although iron stores are intact — mechanism?
tap to flip
Answer
Inflammatory cytokines cause inadequate marrow utilization of iron → a hypoproliferative anemia. Stores are not depleted — ferritin stays normal or increased.
Recall
Iron-deficiency anemia in an adult male or postmenopausal woman → search for?
tap to flip
Answer
Occult GI bleeding (chronic blood loss → microcytic hypochromic anemia).
Recall
Iron-deficiency anemia — FIRST-LINE and ALT?
tap to flip
Answer
Oral iron: ferrous sulfate 300 mg PO TID + identify/stop the bleeding source.
ALT: parenteral iron when oral iron cannot be used/absorbed.
Recall
Anemia of inflammation — FIRST-LINE, ALT, and what to AVOID?
tap to flip
Answer
Treat the underlying disease.
ALT: erythropoietin in appropriate renal/selected hypoproliferative disease.
AVOID routine iron supplementation when true deficiency has not been demonstrated.
Recall
Most-tested complication: iron-deficiency anemia vs. anemia of inflammation?
tap to flip
Answer
IDA: an occult GI malignancy missed as the underlying cause.
AI: persistent symptomatic anemia from uncontrolled underlying disease.
  • ★LIFE-SAVING: severe symptomatic iron-deficiency anemia with hemodynamic compromise → transfusion/resuscitation.
🩺 Think it through
A postmenopausal woman has fatigue, pallor and a microcytic hypochromic anemia with ferritin <15 µg/L and TIBC >360 µg/dL. Oral iron is started. What else must be done?
Search for occult GI bleeding and identify/stop the source — AVOID giving iron indefinitely without investigating unexplained blood loss; the complication to fear is a missed occult GI malignancy.

🧠Megaloblastic Anemias: Vitamin B12 vs. Folate Deficiency11 items▾

Vitamin B12 deficiency vs. folate deficiency
FeatureVitamin B12 deficiencyFolate deficiencyAnswer
Classic vignetteMacrocytic anemia + glossitis + paresthesias, loss of vibration/proprioception, gait disturbanceMalnutrition/alcohol use/malabsorption + macrocytic megaloblastic anemia without neurologic deficits
Smear findingMacrocytosis + hypersegmented neutrophils (>5% of neutrophils with ≥5 lobes, or a single neutrophil with 7 lobes)Macro-ovalocytes + hypersegmented neutrophils
DiscriminatorMethylmalonic acid (MMA) ↑ AND homocysteine ↑Homocysteine ↑ but MMA remains normal
Preferred testSerum B12 + MMA + homocysteineRBC folate (preferred for folate status)
FIRST-LINEVitamin B12 replacement — regimen 100 µg IM daily ×7 days → 100–1000 µg IM monthly; oral alternative 2 mg/day crystalline B12Folic acid 1 mg/day; ALT 5 mg/day for malabsorption
AVOIDTreating undifferentiated megaloblastic anemia with folate alone before excluding B12 deficiencyFolate monotherapy if B12 deficiency has not been excluded
🧠 Memory toolMMA vs. homocysteine (contrast pair)
B12MMA ↑ and homocysteine ↑ + neurologic deficits
FolateHomocysteine ↑ only (MMA normal), no neurologic deficits
MMA is the discriminator: it rises only in B12 deficiency. Serum MMA is raised once B12 deficiency is sufficient to cause anemia or neuropathy, so it settles an equivocal serum B12 level; homocysteine may rise in both B12 and folate deficiency.
Recall
Megaloblastic anemia with ↑ homocysteine but normal MMA and no neurologic deficits → ?
tap to flip
Answer
Folate deficiency.
B12 deficiency would show MMA ↑ + homocysteine ↑ + neurologic deficits.
Board trap · Empiric folateTempting: give folate to an undiagnosed megaloblastic anemia.
Right: empiric folate can normalize the blood count while B12-deficiency neuropathy keeps progressing — B12 status must be excluded before folate is used alone.
  • ✎B12 replacement: µg IM daily × days → 100–1000 µg IM monthly; oral alternative mg/day crystalline B12.
  • ✎Folate deficiency: folic acid mg/day; ALT mg/day for malabsorption.
  • ✎Hypersegmented neutrophils: >% of neutrophils with ≥ lobes, or a single neutrophil with lobes.
Recall
Preferred tests: B12 status vs. folate status?
tap to flip
Answer
B12: serum B12 + MMA + homocysteine.
Folate: RBC folate.
Recall
Neurologic picture that points to B12 rather than folate deficiency?
tap to flip
Answer
Paresthesias, loss of vibration/proprioception, gait disturbance (with macrocytic anemia + glossitis).
Folate deficiency: malnutrition/alcohol use/malabsorption, no neurologic deficits.
  • ★EMERGENCY: severe symptomatic anemia or profound neurologic compromise from B12 deficiency requires immediate replacement/support. Most-tested complication: irreversible neurologic injury.
Recall
Folate deficiency — is it an emergency? Its most-tested pitfall?
tap to flip
Answer
Rarely an emergency by itself — stabilize severe anemia if present.
Pitfall: masking an underlying B12 deficiency while neurologic damage silently progresses.

Marked reticulocytosis — young reticulocytes have relatively higher enzyme activity.

TTP — primary therapy? Where do glucocorticoids fit?
tap to flip
Answer
Prompt plasma exchange — life-saving and still the primary therapy.
Glucocorticoids are adjunctive only; they are not adequate as sole therapy.

Right: TTP is a clinical emergency with very high untreated mortality, and mortality accrues with delay — with a high pretest probability start plasma exchange immediately; the ADAMTS-13 result must not gate treatment, and neither glucocorticoids nor caplacizumab substitutes for it.
🩺 Think it through
A patient develops acute anemia with jaundice, dark urine and reticulocytosis; the smear shows bite cells and Heinz bodies, but a G6PD assay drawn during the episode is normal. What is the diagnosis and the next step?
Oxidant/G6PD hemolysis is still likely — stop/avoid the oxidant trigger + supportive care, and repeat the G6PD assay after the episode resolves (testing during marked reticulocytosis can give a false-negative result).

🌧️Major Depressive Disorder10 items▾

Major depressive disorder — rapid-review targets
Rapid-review targetBoard answerAnswer
Classic vignette opener≥2 weeks of depressed mood/anhedonia + sleep/appetite change, fatigue, guilt, poor concentration ± suicidality
Diagnostic criteria≥5 of 9 symptoms for ≥2 weeks, with depressed mood OR anhedonia required as a core symptom
Gold-standard testClinical diagnosis — no laboratory/imaging gold standard
First evaluation prioritySuicide risk + history of mania/hypomania
FIRST-LINE / ALTSSRI first-line; ALT = SNRI, bupropion, mirtazapine, selected TCA; combine with psychotherapy
AVOIDAntidepressant monotherapy if bipolar disorder is suspected
LIFE-SAVINGActive suicidal intent/plan/means → urgent psychiatric evaluation + hospitalization when unsafe
🧠 Memory toolThe nine screening symptoms of depression
DDepressed mood
SSleep change
IInterest lost — anhedonia
GGuilt / worthlessness
EEnergy low — fatigue
CConcentration poor / indecision
AAppetite / weight change
PPsychomotor change
SSuicide — thoughts of death/suicide
Depressed mood + SIG E CAPS = 9 symptoms. Depressed mood or anhedonia must be one of them.
  • ✎MDD = of 9 symptoms for , with depressed mood OR required as a core symptom.
Recall
Before starting an antidepressant, what two things must be evaluated first?
tap to flip
Answer
Suicide risk + any history of mania/hypomania.
  • ✎Assess antidepressant response after roughly at a target therapeutic dose before labeling an uncomplicated treatment failure.
Recall
Only partial improvement after an adequate, well-tolerated antidepressant trial → next step?
tap to flip
Answer
Increase the dose to optimize the therapeutic response.
  • ✎After remission, continue antidepressant treatment for approximately ; recurrent episodes may need longer maintenance.
Recall
Severe/treatment-resistant depression (psychotic features, marked incapacity, repeated medication failure) → treatment?
tap to flip
Answer
Still starts with antidepressant + psychotherapy.
ECT is the listed option for resistant disease or when medication is medically unsuitable.
Recall
Most-tested complication of depression — and the question every depressed patient must be asked?
tap to flip
Answer
Completed suicide. Ask every depressed patient directly about suicidal thoughts.
Board trap · "Depression" hiding bipolar disorder"Depression" + a past week of decreased need for sleep, grandiosity and excessive activity = bipolar depression, not straightforward unipolar MDD. Tempting: start an antidepressant alone. Antidepressant monotherapy is the wrong answer here.

🧠Schizophrenia8 items▾

Schizophrenia — rapid-review targets
Rapid-review targetBoard answerAnswer
Classic vignette openerYoung adult with social withdrawal followed by hallucinations, delusions, disorganized thinking ± negative symptoms
DurationCore syndrome persists ≥6 months
First diagnostic priorityExclude delirium, drugs/substances, and neurologic/medical disease
FIRST-LINE / ALTSecond-generation antipsychotic first-line; conventional antipsychotic as ALT depending on context
Treatment-resistant diseaseClozapine
AVOIDLabeling new psychosis as schizophrenia before excluding substance/medical causes
LIFE-SAVINGDangerous psychosis, command hallucinations, or inability to self-care → hospitalization + acute antipsychotic treatment
🧠 Memory toolPositive vs negative symptoms (contrast pair)
+Positive (added): hallucinations, delusions, disorganized thought/speech
−Negative (taken away): avolition, anhedonia, reduced emotional expression, social withdrawal
Positive = something added to experience; negative = something missing.
  • ✎Negative symptoms predominate in about of patients with schizophrenia and are associated with long-term outcome and poorer response to drug treatment.
Schizophrenia look-alikes
DiagnosisDeciding featureAnswer
SchizophreniaCore syndrome persists ≥6 months
Brief psychotic disorderLasts <1 month
Schizophreniform disorderSchizophrenia-like illness that has not yet reached the ≥6-month duration — lasts ≥1 month but <6 months
Schizoaffective disorderA major mood syndrome with a substantial independent relationship to the psychosis
Recall
New psychosis — what must be done before calling it schizophrenia?
tap to flip
Answer
Exclude delirium, drugs/substances, and neurologic/medical disease first. Do not label new psychosis as schizophrenia before that.
Recall
Most-tested complication of schizophrenia?
tap to flip
Answer
Suicide.
Board trap · Delirium mislabeled as schizophreniaFluctuating consciousness + impaired attention = delirium, not primary schizophrenia. Tempting: diagnose a new psychotic disorder. Right: always exclude a medical cause before diagnosing a new psychotic disorder.
🩺 Think it through
A young adult with schizophrenia hears voices commanding him to act and can no longer care for himself. What is the life-saving step?
Hospitalization + acute antipsychotic treatment — dangerous psychosis, command hallucinations, or inability to self-care all require it.

💊Antipsychotic Adverse-Effect Patterns7 items▾

Antipsychotic adverse effects — finding, mechanism, action
FindingMechanism / ThinkBoard actionAnswer
Acute dystoniaDopamine blockadeAnticholinergic treatment
AkathisiaInner restlessnessAdjust drug; symptom-directed therapy
ParkinsonismTremor/rigidity/bradykinesiaDose/drug adjustment ± anticholinergic
Tardive dyskinesiaChronic involuntary orofacial/distal movementsReassess the antipsychotic; avoid simply adding an anticholinergic
Weight gain / diabetesEspecially clozapine/olanzapineMonitor weight, glucose, lipids
AgranulocytosisClozapineHematologic monitoring; urgent evaluation for infection symptoms

Recall
On an antipsychotic: fever + rigidity + autonomic instability → think? do?
tap to flip
Answer
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome → STOP the antipsychotic immediately.
  • ✎Tardive dyskinesia occurs in up to approximately of patients after prolonged -antipsychotic exposure.
Recall
Clozapine — its role, and why it is not a casual first choice?
tap to flip
Answer
The high-yield drug for treatment-resistant schizophrenia.
Agranulocytosis, seizures and metabolic toxicity make it a monitored therapy, not a casual first choice.
A substantial proportion of patients unresponsive to conventional antipsychotics respond better to it, and it has demonstrated superiority in preventing suicide; blood-dyscrasia risk limits it to selected cases.
Recall
Which antipsychotics especially cause weight gain/diabetes, and what is monitored?
tap to flip
Answer
Especially clozapine/olanzapine. Monitor weight, glucose, lipids.
🧠 Memory toolAnticholinergic: acute dystonia vs tardive dyskinesia (contrast pair)
AcuteAcute dystonia (dopamine blockade) → anticholinergic fixes it
TardiveTardive dyskinesia (chronic involuntary orofacial/distal movements) → anticholinergic does not fix it; reassess the antipsychotic
Acute = Add anticholinergic. Tardive = Think again about the antipsychotic.
Board trap · Anticholinergic for tardive dyskinesiaTempting: "treat" tardive dyskinesia by simply adding an anticholinergic. Right: reassess the antipsychotic itself. Anticholinergics fix acute dystonia, not tardive dyskinesia.

😰Anxiety Disorders: Panic Disorder & GAD7 items▾

Panic disorder vs generalized anxiety disorder
FeaturePanic disorderGeneralized anxiety disorder (GAD)Answer
Classic vignette openerSudden unexplained palpitations, dyspnea, chest discomfort, trembling, dizziness, fear of dying; repeated normal cardiac workupsWorry about finances, family, health, and work throughout the day, with insomnia and muscle tension
Course / criteriaAttack peaks within ~10 minutes; recurrent attacks + ≥1 month of worry about further attacks or maladaptive behavior changePersistent multidomain worry, restlessness, impaired concentration, muscle tension, autonomic symptoms, insomnia (no full DSM count/duration rule is given)
FIRST-LINE / ALTSSRI; short-term benzodiazepine as ALT for selected severe patients while awaiting antidepressant effectPsychotherapy + SSRI (or SNRI); buspirone ALT, needs ~2 weeks for benefit
AVOIDLong-term benzodiazepine dependence; diagnosing panic at the first unexplained chest pain/dyspnea episodeChronic indiscriminate benzodiazepine use or abrupt discontinuation
Most-tested complicationAgoraphobiaMajor depressive disorder / benzodiazepine dependence
Panic mimics and their discriminators
Panic mimicDiscriminatorAnswer
SVTDocumented tachyarrhythmia
HyperthyroidismPersistent tremor/weight loss + abnormal thyroid tests
PheochromocytomaEpisodic hypertension + metanephrine excess
HypoglycemiaDocumented low glucose
Stimulant useCocaine/amphetamine/sympathomimetic exposure
  • ✎A panic attack peaks within about ; panic disorder = recurrent attacks + of worry about further attacks or maladaptive behavior change.
Recall
GAD alternative drug that is not a benzodiazepine — and how long until benefit?
tap to flip
Answer
Buspirone — needs ~2 weeks for benefit.
Recall
Most-tested complication: panic disorder vs GAD?
tap to flip
Answer
Panic disorder → agoraphobia.
GAD → major depressive disorder / benzodiazepine dependence.
🩺 Think it through
A patient has a first episode of unexplained chest pain and dyspnea; panic is suspected. What must be ordered before labeling it panic?
ECG, glucose, and thyroid testing (± toxicology) to exclude medical mimics before calling a first episode panic.
Board trap · "Panic" before the medical emergencyTempting: call chest pain/dyspnea "panic". Right: first exclude ACS, arrhythmia, hypoglycemia, thyrotoxicosis, or intoxication/withdrawal — always exclude the medical emergency first.

LIFE-SAVINGSevere mania + psychosis/aggression/inability to self-care → hospitalization + mood stabilizer ± antipsychotic

Mood stabilizerHarrison therapeutic rangeAnswer

🧠 Memory toolFeatures of mania (DIG FAST)
DDistractibility
IIndiscretion — reckless spending/sexual behavior
GGrandiosity
FFlight of ideas — racing thoughts
AActivity ↑ — excessive energy

Recall
Earliest classic clue of mania?
tap to flip
Answer
Decreased need for sleep without fatigue.
  • ✎Therapeutic ranges: lithium mEq/L, valproate µg/mL, carbamazepine µg/mL.
  • ✎Acute mania: lithium may take to work — is used adjunctively for agitation, with an added for severe agitation that responds only partially.
  • ✎Rapid cycling = or more mood episodes within a year; in some bipolar patients it is precipitated or worsened by prolonged treatment.
Recall
When may valproate outperform lithium?
tap to flip
Answer
In rapid cycling or mixed/dysphoric mania — valproic acid may be more effective than lithium there, even though lithium is the gold-standard mood stabilizer overall.
Recall
Lithium toxicity — features and usual precipitants?
tap to flip
Answer
Vomiting, worsening tremor, confusion/ataxia.
Often precipitated by dehydration, renal dysfunction, NSAID, or thiazide use.
Recall
How is lithium toxicity diagnosed, and what else is checked?
tap to flip
Answer
Serum lithium level interpreted alongside clinical status and renal function.
Check creatinine/eGFR, electrolytes, thyroid function, and calcium.
Recall
Lithium toxicity → FIRST-LINE management?
tap to flip
Answer
Stop lithium + correct volume/electrolyte abnormalities.
  • ★Severe lithium toxicity is a medical emergency; dialysis may be required depending on clinical/renal status.
Recall
Chronic adverse effects of lithium?
tap to flip
Answer
Hypothyroidism, nephrogenic diabetes insipidus/polyuria, renal dysfunction, weight gain, and hypercalcemia.
Board trap · NSAID or thiazide added to lithiumTempting: add an NSAID or a thiazide to a lithium regimen without a second thought. Right: both can raise lithium levels and precipitate toxicity — consider lithium-level elevation.

🧼Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder8 items▾

🩺 Think it through
A patient knows the contamination fear is excessive but washes hands repeatedly, or repeatedly checks locks, to relieve anxiety. What is the diagnosis?
Obsessive-compulsive disorder — the classic opener: ego-dystonic intrusive obsession + anxiety-relieving repetitive compulsion.
🧠 Memory toolObsession vs compulsion (contrast pair)
OObsession — ego-dystonic, intrusive (the patient knows the fear is excessive)
CCompulsion — repetitive act (washing, checking locks) that relieves the anxiety
  • ★Harrison requires obsessions and/or compulsions that impair everyday functioning; a complete DSM numeric time criterion is not given.
Recall
OCD → first-line drug, first-line psychotherapy, alternative drug?
tap to flip
Answer
FIRST-LINE drug = SSRI.
FIRST-LINE psychotherapy = cognitive-behavioral therapy with exposure-response prevention (ERP).
ALT drug = clomipramine.
Recall
OCD → what to AVOID?
tap to flip
Answer
AVOID benzodiazepine monotherapy, and avoid encouraging avoidance of feared situations or participation in rituals.
Recall
OCD → when is urgent psychiatric care needed?
tap to flip
Answer
Severe self-neglect, inability to eat/drink, self-injury, or suicidality → urgent psychiatric care.
Recall
Most-tested complication of OCD?
tap to flip
Answer
Major depression / severe functional impairment.
Board trap · OCD obsession vs psychotic delusionAn OCD obsession is intrusive and unwanted, with a compulsion that relieves anxiety. A delusion is typically a fixed conviction without that obsession-compulsion relief cycle. Do not call an obsession a delusion.

Suicide risk — rapid-review targets
Rapid-review targetBoard answerAnswer
Classic vignette openerDepressed/psychotic/intoxicated patient says life is not worth living and has obtained a lethal means
Most important "test"Directly ask: thoughts → plan → intent → access to means → prior attempts
Gold-standard testClinical structured risk assessment
FIRST-LINEEnsure safety, continuous supervision as required, urgent psychiatric assessment
AVOIDReassurance and routine outpatient discharge despite an active plan/intent

🧠 Memory toolSuicide risk — the 5 direct questions, in order
1Thoughts
2Plan
3Intent
4Access to means
5Prior attempts
Number hook: five direct questions, from thought to past action.
Recall
Besides depression, what further raises concern for suicide?
tap to flip
Answer
Psychosis, severe agitation, intoxication, a recent attempt, hopelessness, and inability to cooperate with safety planning.
Every depressed patient should be asked directly about suicide.
🩺 Think it through
A depressed patient says life is not worth living, has obtained a lethal means, and has an active plan/intent. Reassure and discharge to routine outpatient care, or what else?
Remove means + protect the patient + hospitalize when safety cannot be ensured. AVOID reassurance and routine outpatient discharge despite an active plan/intent.
  • ★Acute agitation/dangerous psychosis — first step: safety + ABCs + vitals + glucose + oxygenation + evaluate for a medical/substance cause.
Recall
Agitation → FIRST-LINE and ALT?
tap to flip
Answer
FIRST-LINE = verbal de-escalation + low-stimulation environment when feasible.
ALT = antipsychotic and/or benzodiazepine chosen by likely cause.
Recall
When is immediate containment/hospitalization needed?
tap to flip
Answer
Immediately when danger to self or others cannot otherwise be controlled.
Board trap · Agitated patient with fluctuating attentionFluctuating attention/consciousness in an agitated patient → treat as delirium until proved otherwise, not as a primary psychiatric disorder.

🎯Psychiatry Rapid-Fire Board Traps8 items▾

Board trap · MDD vs bipolar≥5 depressive symptoms × ≥2 weeks = MDD. But depression + prior decreased sleep/grandiosity = bipolar disorder, not unipolar MDD.
Board trap · Schizophrenia vs deliriumHallucinations/delusions ≥6 months with no medical cause = schizophrenia. New psychosis + fluctuating attention = delirium — find the medical cause.
Recall
Sudden fear + palpitations peaking in ~10 minutes vs persistent all-day multidomain worry?
tap to flip
Answer
Peaks in ~10 minutes = panic attack.
Persistent all-day multidomain worry = GAD.
Board trap · Mania and antidepressantsLittle sleep + grandiosity + pressured speech = mania, treated with a mood stabilizer — never antidepressant monotherapy.
Board trap · Lithium + thiazide/NSAIDLithium patient + thiazide/NSAID + tremor/confusion = lithium toxicity, not a routine dose increase.
Recall
Intrusive contamination fear + repetitive washing → diagnosis and treatment?
tap to flip
Answer
OCD → SSRI + ERP, not benzodiazepine monotherapy.
Board trap · NMS — do not rechallengeAntipsychotic + rigidity + fever + CK ↑ = NMS — stop the antipsychotic; do not continue or rechallenge it.
Board trap · Suicidal plan + intent + meansSuicidal plan + intent + accessible means = hospital-level safety, not routine outpatient reassurance.

🚨Acute Kidney Injury (AKI)14 items▾

AKI — rapid-review targets
Rapid-review targetBoard answerAnswer
Classic vignette openerHospitalized/septic/dehydrated patient with rising creatinine ± oliguria
KDIGO diagnosis (supplementary)SCr ↑ ≥0.3 mg/dL within 48 h, OR ≥1.5× baseline within 7 d, OR urine output <0.5 mL/kg/h for ≥6 h
First testsUA + microscopy, creatinine/electrolytes, urine output, drug/volume review
FIRST-LINECorrect the underlying cause: perfusion, nephrotoxins, infection, or obstruction
AVOID"Renal-dose" dopamine; blind fluid loading
LIFE-SAVINGDialysis for refractory hyperkalemia, acidosis, pulmonary edema, or severe uremic complications
  • ✎KDIGO AKI: SCr ↑ ≥ mg/dL within , OR ≥ baseline within 7 d, OR urine output <0.5 mL/kg/h for ≥6 h.
  • ★AKI approach: Identify insult → FeNa / urine microscopy → Classify prerenal / ATN / postrenal → Treat the cause
Prerenal vs ATN vs postrenal
FindingPrerenalATNPostrenalAnswer
FeNa<1%>1% typicalVariable
Urine Na<10 mmol/L>20 mmol/LVariable
Urine osmolality>500 mOsm/kg<300 mOsm/kgVariable
SedimentBland/hyalineMuddy-brown granular castsOften bland
Decisive testClinical responseUrine microscopyUltrasound/obstruction imaging
Recall
BUN-to-creatinine ratio in prerenal azotemia — value and reason?
tap to flip
Answer
>20:1. With decreased effective renal perfusion the intact tubules avidly reabsorb sodium and water, and urea reabsorption rises disproportionately.
It travels with the rest of the prerenal pattern after volume loss: low urine sodium (usually <20 mEq/L), concentrated urine with high osmolality, bland sediment.
Board trap · Low FeNa = always prerenalTempting: treat FeNa <1% as proof of prerenal azotemia. Right: too absolute — contrast nephropathy and several other intrinsic processes can also show a low FeNa. Read FeNa together with the clinical setting, urine sediment, and other data.
Recall
Muddy-brown granular casts → ?
tap to flip
Answer
ATN — urine microscopy is the decisive test.
Recall
Most-tested complication of AKI?
tap to flip
Answer
Hyperkalemia
Recall
Postrenal AKI with significant obstruction → life-saving step?
tap to flip
Answer
LIFE-SAVING: decompression — Foley catheter, ureteral stent, or nephrostomy, depending on the level of obstruction.
Distended bladder + bilateral hydronephrosis = bladder outlet obstruction → insert a bladder catheter first, immediately.
Board trap · Normal ultrasound = no obstructionTempting: exclude postrenal AKI because the renal ultrasound shows no hydronephrosis. Right: in early obstruction, or when the ureter cannot dilate, collecting-system dilation may not yet be present — a negative ultrasound can coexist with clinically important obstruction.
🧠 Memory toolIndications for dialysis (complications, not a creatinine number)
AAcidosis — refractory
EElectrolytes — refractory hyperkalemia
IIntoxication (dialyzable toxins)
OOverload — pulmonary edema
UUremia — uremic encephalopathy / severe uremic complications
AEIOU. Dialysis is started for complications, never for a fixed creatinine cut-off.
Board trap · Dialysis by creatinine numberTempting: start dialysis once creatinine passes a threshold. Right: dialysis is started based on complications (refractory hyperK, acidosis, pulmonary edema, uremic encephalopathy), never a fixed creatinine cut-off.
Board trap · "Renal-dose" dopamineTempting: a low-dose dopamine drip to "protect" the kidney. Right: Harrison rejects this as therapy — AVOID. AKI management means fixing the cause (perfusion, nephrotoxin, infection, obstruction), never a dopamine drip. Blind fluid loading is also to be avoided.
🩺 Think it through
A hospitalized septic patient has rising creatinine and oliguria; FeNa is >1%, urine osmolality <300 mOsm/kg, and the sediment shows muddy-brown granular casts. What is the type of AKI and the management principle?
ATN. Correct the underlying cause (perfusion, nephrotoxins, infection, obstruction); no "renal-dose" dopamine or blind fluid loading; dialysis only for refractory complications.

⏳Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD)12 items▾

Recall
Classic CKD vignette?
tap to flip
Answer
Long-standing diabetes/hypertension with chronically elevated creatinine plus anemia, pruritus, edema, or small kidneys.
  • ✎CKD (KDIGO 2024, supplementary): kidney structure/function abnormality present ≥, defined by eGFR < mL/min/1.73 m² OR ≥ marker of kidney damage.
  • ✎Albuminuria categories: A1 < mg/g, A2 mg/g, A3 > mg/g.
CKD GFR categories
CategoryeGFR (mL/min/1.73 m²)Answer
G1≥90 + kidney-damage marker
G260–89 + kidney-damage marker
G3a45–59
G3b30–44
G415–29
G5<15
🧠 Memory toolCKD G-stage cut-offs (number hook)
90G1 ≥90 — needs a kidney-damage marker
60G2 60–89 — needs a kidney-damage marker
45G3a 45–59
30G3b 30–44
15G4 15–29; G5 <15
90 → 60 → 45 → 30 → 15. G1 and G2 count as CKD only with a kidney-damage marker.
Recall
CKD: first-line disease modification?
tap to flip
Answer
Control the underlying cause and blood pressure; ACE inhibitor or ARB, especially for proteinuric disease.
Recall
CKD add-ons (ALT): what treats what?
tap to flip
Answer
Diuretics → volume overload
Bicarbonate → chronic acidosis
Phosphate binders
Iron/ESA → selected anemia
Recall
Advanced CKD → secondary hyperparathyroidism: mechanism?
tap to flip
Answer
Declining GFR → phosphate retention and ↑ FGF-23 → reduced renal 1α-hydroxylase activity and ↓ calcitriol → lower ionized calcium. All of these stimulate PTH secretion and parathyroid growth; phosphate also acts directly on the parathyroid gland.
Recall
CKD: life-saving indications for dialysis?
tap to flip
Answer
LIFE-SAVING: refractory volume overload, hyperkalemia/acidosis, encephalopathy, pericarditis/serositis, or severe symptomatic uremia.
Recall
Most-tested complications of CKD?
tap to flip
Answer
Cardiovascular disease and hyperkalemia.
Recall
Why is overt hyperkalemia a late event in CKD?
tap to flip
Answer
The remaining nephrons increase distal potassium secretion (aldosterone-driven) and gastrointestinal (colonic) potassium excretion rises, so plasma K stays relatively preserved despite a falling GFR.
Board trap · A number triggers dialysisTempting: start dialysis because of an eGFR or BUN/creatinine value. Right: a number alone never triggers dialysis in CKD — the decision is driven by refractory complications (volume overload, hyperK, acidosis, encephalopathy, serositis), exactly as in AKI.

🧂Sodium Disorders: Hyponatremia & Hypernatremia10 items▾

Hyponatremia vs hypernatremia
FeatureHyponatremiaHypernatremiaAnswer
CutoffNa <135 mmol/LNa >145 mmol/L (supplementary)
Classic vignetteConfusion/seizure on hypotonic fluid, thiazide, SIADH-inducing drug, CHF/cirrhosis, or volume lossFrail/altered patient unable to drink, or DI patient with polyuria
Severe clueNeurologic disease, Na <120 mmol/L and/or rapid fallHypertonicity with neurologic dysfunction
FIRST-LINE (severe)Hypertonic salineFree-water replacement
FIRST-LINE by subtype0.9% saline for hypovolemic diseaseDesmopressin for central DI

Recall
Hyponatremia + urine osmolality <100 mOsm/kg → ?
tap to flip
Answer
Appropriate AVP suppression — think polydipsia or low-solute intake, not SIADH.
  • ✎Maximum correction of chronic hyponatremia: ≤ mmol/L in the first 24 h; ≤ mmol/L in the first 48 h.
Recall
Central vs nephrogenic DI — the discriminator?
tap to flip
Answer
Central DI: dilute polyuria that responds to desmopressin.
Nephrogenic DI: dilute polyuria that persists despite desmopressin (DDAVP).
Recall
Nephrogenic DI → treatment (ALT)?
tap to flip
Answer
Thiazide, or amiloride particularly for lithium-associated disease.
Recall
Hyponatremic seizure/coma → ?
tap to flip
Answer
LIFE-SAVING: controlled hypertonic saline.
Recall
Hemodynamically unstable hypernatremia → order of steps?
tap to flip
Answer
Restore circulation first, then correct the free-water deficit.
🧠 Memory toolToo-fast sodium correction (contrast pair)
Low → up too fastChronic hyponatremia corrected too quickly → osmotic demyelination syndrome
High → down too fastLongstanding hypernatremia corrected too quickly → cerebral edema
AVOID rapid correction in both directions.
Board trap · Chasing a normal sodium too fastTempting: normalize the sodium quickly. Right: correcting chronic hyponatremia faster than 10–12 mmol/L per 24 h (or hypernatremia too quickly) causes osmotic demyelination or cerebral edema instead of curing the patient.
🩺 Think it through
A patient on a thiazide is brought in seizing with Na <120 mmol/L. What is given, and what limit applies if the hyponatremia is chronic?
Controlled hypertonic saline (life-saving). Limit correction of chronic hyponatremia to ≤10–12 mmol/L in the first 24 h and ≤18 mmol/L in the first 48 h to avoid osmotic demyelination.

Classic hypokalemia vignette?
tap to flip

Diuretic/vomiting/diarrhea patient with weakness, cramps, or arrhythmia.

Ventricular arrhythmia.
