FIRST-LINE emergencyIV calcium for membrane stabilization (10 mL 10% calcium gluconate over 10 min)
Shift K intracellularlyIV insulin 10 U + glucose ± nebulized albuterol 10–20 mg
Remove KDiuretic, binder, or dialysis
AVOIDAssuming a normal ECG means hyperK is safe
LIFE-SAVINGRefractory severe hyperK → hemodialysis
Recall
CKD on RAS blockade + a potassium-sparing agent: why is a dietary potassium load hazardous?
tap to flip
Answer
CKD already reduces the renal reserve for potassium excretion; RAS blockade and potassium-sparing agents further impair distal potassium secretion — the drug effect is superimposed on the kidney's limited capacity, so K rises disproportionately.
  • ★Hyperkalemia sequence: CALCIUM — membrane stabilize → SHIFT — insulin/glucose ± albuterol → REMOVE — diuretic/binder/dialysis
🧠 Memory toolEmergency hyperkalemia doses — "rule of 10s"
10 mLof calcium gluconate
10%calcium gluconate concentration
10 mininfusion time for the calcium
10 UIV insulin, with glucose
10–20 mgnebulized albuterol (optional add-on)
Calcium stabilizes the membrane first; insulin/glucose ± albuterol shift K into cells.
  • ✎Hyperkalemia: diagnostic cutoff K ≥ mmol/L; emergency threshold K ≥ mmol/L and/or ECG changes.
Recall
ECG progression in hyperkalemia?
tap to flip
Answer
Peaked T → PR ↑ → QRS widening → P loss → sine wave
Board trap · Normal ECG = safe hyperKTempting: withhold treatment because the ECG is normal. Right: AVOID assuming a normal ECG means hyperkalemia is safe — K ≥6.0 mmol/L is an emergency threshold with or without ECG changes.
Board trap · IV calcium in digoxin toxicityTempting: reflex IV calcium for every hyperkalemic patient. Right: with significant digoxin toxicity Harrison flags the combination as dangerous — AVOID it or give with extreme caution.
🩺 Think it through
A CKD patient on an ACE inhibitor and an MRA presents with weakness, K ≥6.0 mmol/L and peaked T waves. What is given first, and what follows?
IV calcium first (10 mL 10% calcium gluconate over 10 min) for membrane stabilization → shift with IV insulin 10 U + glucose ± nebulized albuterol → remove with diuretic, binder, or dialysis; refractory severe hyperK → hemodialysis.

⚗️Acid–Base Disorders15 items▾

Metabolic acidosis vs metabolic alkalosis
FeatureMetabolic AcidosisMetabolic AlkalosisAnswer
Classic vignetteDKA/sepsis/renal failure/diarrhea with low HCO₃⁻ and compensatory tachypneaRepeated vomiting/NG suction or diuretic use with hypokalemia
Key discriminatorAnion gap = Na − (Cl + HCO₃)Urine chloride
CutoffsNormal pH 7.35–7.45; AG >12 mmol/L = elevatedUrine Cl <20 mEq/L = chloride-responsive; >20 mEq/L = chloride-resistant
FIRST-LINETreat the underlying causeChloride-responsive: normal saline + KCl
AVOIDRoutine bicarbonate for every high-AG acidosisBlind saline for chloride-resistant/mineralocorticoid alkalosis
Most-tested complicationHyperkalemia / cardiovascular instabilityHypokalemic arrhythmia
Anion gap
AG = Na − (Cl + HCO₃)
AG >12 mmol/L = elevated. Normal pH 7.35–7.45.
Na 140, Cl 100, HCO₃ 10 → 140 − (100 + 10) = 30 → elevated
Albumin-corrected anion gap
Corrected AG ≈ measured AG + 2.5 × (4 − albumin in g/dL)
Low albumin hides an elevated gap.
Measured AG 12, albumin 2 g/dL → 12 + 2.5 × (4 − 2) = 12 + 5 = 17
Winter formula (expected respiratory compensation)
Expected PaCO₂ = 1.5 × (HCO₃) + 8 ± 2
Predicts the PaCO₂ expected for a given HCO₃ in metabolic acidosis.
HCO₃ 10 → 1.5 × 10 + 8 = 23 → expected PaCO₂ 21–25 mmHg
Recall
High-anion-gap acidosis — causes?
tap to flip
Answer
DKA, lactate, renal failure, toxins.
Recall
Normal-anion-gap acidosis — causes?
tap to flip
Answer
Diarrhea, RTA, early CKD, saline.

MMethanol (toxin)
UUremia — renal failure
DDiabetic ketoacidosis
PPropylene glycol / paraldehyde (toxin)
IIsoniazid / iron (toxin)

Recall
Classic acid–base picture of adult salicylate intoxication?
tap to flip
Answer
Respiratory alkalosis, or a mixed respiratory alkalosis + high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis — low PaCO₂ and low HCO₃⁻ with a pH that can look near normal.

Recall
Metabolic alkalosis that persists after the vomiting has stopped — what maintains it?
tap to flip
Answer
Generated by HCl loss, then maintained by extracellular volume contraction plus chloride and potassium depletion, which enhance renal bicarbonate reabsorption (urine chloride is very low).
  • ✎Bicarbonate is a reasonable ALT in selected severe/chronic acidosis — Harrison treats chronic HCO₃⁻ < mmol/L.
Recall
Severe acidemia with shock/renal failure → ?
tap to flip
Answer
LIFE-SAVING: treat the cause ± dialysis/support.
Recall
Severe alkalemia with arrhythmia/seizure → ?
tap to flip
Answer
Monitored correction of the cause and electrolytes.
Board trap · Reflex bicarbonateTempting: bicarbonate for every high-anion-gap acidosis. Right: it is reserved for selected severe/chronic cases, not routine DKA or lactic acidosis — treat the underlying cause.
Board trap · Blind saline in alkalosisTempting: normal saline for every metabolic alkalosis. Right: saline + KCl works only for chloride-responsive disease (urine Cl <20 mEq/L); AVOID blind saline for chloride-resistant/mineralocorticoid alkalosis.

Board trap · Nitrofurantoin for pyelonephritisTempting: continue nitrofurantoin when fever/flank pain appear. Right: it treats cystitis but never achieves adequate renal parenchymal tissue levels for upper-tract infection — change therapy.
Board trap · Treating the culture, not the patientTempting: antibiotics because the urine culture is positive. Board trap · Catheter + fever + bacteriuria = CAUTITempting: attribute any fever in a catheterized patient with bacteriuria to the catheter. Right: bacteriuria and pyuria are common and nonspecific in catheterized patients — another clear source of fever substantially weakens the attribution to CAUTI.

A woman started on nitrofurantoin for dysuria returns with fever, flank/CVA pain and vomiting. What is the diagnosis and what must change?
Acute pyelonephritis. Stop relying on nitrofurantoin (inadequate renal parenchymal levels); outpatient option is ciprofloxacin 500 mg BID × 7 d if susceptible. With sepsis or infected obstruction: IV antibiotics, resuscitation, urgent drainage if obstructed.

A patient has cola-colored urine, periorbital edema and hypertension 2 weeks after impetigo; complement is low. What is the diagnosis, is biopsy needed, and what is the treatment?
PSGN. Biopsy is not routine in a classic case (only if atypical/severe). Supportive volume/BP management and treatment of any persistent strep infection — no routine immunosuppression.

tap to flip

🩺 Think it through
A patient presents with hemoptysis, RBC casts and a rapidly rising creatinine; serologies are still pending. What is the next move?
Treat now as pulmonary-renal syndrome / RPGN — do not delay therapy (plasma exchange/immunosuppression) for the full work-up; ICU/nephrology ± dialysis for alveolar hemorrhage or severe renal failure. Renal biopsy + disease-specific serology is the gold standard.

A child develops abrupt nephrotic syndrome with normal complement and little/no hematuria. Is a biopsy needed before treatment, and what is first-line?
Minimal change disease. The classic childhood picture may be treated empirically (biopsy only when required) with a glucocorticoid; steroid-sparing agents (calcineurin inhibitor/rituximab) for frequent relapse/refractory disease.

Sudden severe colicky flank pain radiating to the groin, with restlessness and nausea/vomiting ± hematuria. No finding is pathognomonic.
  • ✎Stone composition: approximately calcium, struvite, uric acid, and 1% cystine.
🧠 Memory toolStone composition (number hook)
75Calcium
15Struvite
5Uric acid
1Cystine
75 – 15 – 5 – 1, most to least common.
  • ✎First-line prevention across stone types starts with fluid intake of L/day.
  • ✎Uric acid stone: potassium citrate to urine pH ± allopurinol.
Recall
Stone with an infected, obstructed collecting system → ?
tap to flip
Answer
IV antibiotics plus urgent stent or nephrostomy.
Recall
Most-tested complication of nephrolithiasis?
tap to flip
Answer
Obstructive infected hydronephrosis/urosepsis.
Recall
Calcium oxalate vs uric acid stone on imaging and urine?
tap to flip
Answer
Calcium oxalate: most common, radiopaque.
Uric acid: radiolucent, acidic urine, gout-associated, prevented by alkalinizing the urine.
Board trap · Restricting dietary calciumTempting: tell a calcium stone former to cut dietary calcium. Right: indiscriminate dietary calcium restriction is wrong — AVOID; sodium restriction, thiazides, and citrate are the evidence-based moves for hypercalciuria.
Why: adequate dietary calcium binds oxalate in the gut and reduces its absorption — higher dietary calcium is associated with lower stone risk, whereas a low-calcium diet raises urinary oxalate and calcium oxalate stone risk and may also worsen bone density.

Recall
Gout + acidic-urine stone → which stone, and how is it managed?
tap to flip

Uric acid stone — managed by alkalinizing the urine.
Recall
Struvite vs cystine stone — clues and management?

Struvite: staghorn calculus, alkaline urine, urease-producing organism → infection control plus complete removal.

Board trap · Last-minute "do not pick" listAll classic wrong answers:
• Ignoring thrombosis risk in nephrotic syndrome
• Assuming steroid-resistant disease is still MCD
• Glucocorticoid monotherapy for membranous nephropathy
• Waiting for the full RCC triad
• Empiric fluoroquinolones for gonorrhea
• Avoiding penicillin instead of desensitizing in pregnant syphilis
• Telling a patient antivirals cure latent HSV
• Treating an infected obstructed stone with antibiotics alone, without drainage

🫁Acute Respiratory Failure — ARDS & Hypercapnic Failure18 items▾

ARDS rapid review
ARDS rapid-reviewBoard answerAnswer
Classic vignetteSepsis / pneumonia / aspiration patient develops severe hypoxemia + bilateral infiltrates
ARDS criteriaAcute onset ≤1 week + bilateral diffuse infiltrates + PaO₂/FiO₂ ↓ ≤300 + failure not primarily explained by elevated left-atrial pressure
Ventilator FIRST-LINETidal volume ≤6 mL/kg predicted body weight; plateau pressure ≤30 cm H₂O
Preferred ALTPEEP, prone positioning; ECMO reserved for selected refractory cases
🧠 Memory toolARDS by the numbers
≤1 weekAcute onset
≤300PaO₂/FiO₂
≤6 mL/kgTidal volume (predicted body weight)
≤30 cm H₂OPlateau pressure
88–95%SpO₂ target on the ventilator
Small breaths, low pressures, modest oxygen target.
  • ✎Harrison: hypoxemic respiratory failure = SaO₂ below % despite increased FiO₂.
Recall
Hypoxemia that barely improves on high FiO₂ → which mechanism, and why?
tap to flip
Answer
Intrapulmonary (right-to-left) shunt. Shunted blood reaches the arterial circulation without contacting ventilated alveoli, so raising inspired oxygen gives only limited correction. ARDS / severe alveolar filling leaves lung units perfused but poorly or not ventilated → oxygen-resistant hypoxemia.
Recall
Gold-standard test for ARDS?
tap to flip
Answer
None — there is no single gold-standard test. Diagnosis is clinical-radiographic plus the P/F ratio.
  • ✎Target oxygenation during ARDS ventilation: SpO₂ % — not full normalization.
Board trap · High tidal volumes in ARDSAVOID high tidal volumes / excessive plateau pressures — the classic wrong-answer ventilator strategy. Low tidal volumes are central to lung protection because they reduce overdistention and ventilator-induced lung injury (lower plateau and driving pressure). Permissive hypercapnia is accepted when necessary — do not raise tidal volume or airway pressure just to normalize PaCO₂.
Recall
ARDS with refractory hypoxemia or exhaustion → ?
tap to flip
Answer
LIFE-SAVING territory: intubate for lung-protective ventilation.
Recall
Most-tested complications of ARDS?
tap to flip
Answer
Barotrauma/pneumothorax or multiorgan failure.
Recall
Defining physiology of hypercapnic respiratory failure?
tap to flip
Answer
Alveolar hypoventilation → PaCO₂ ↑ + pH ↓.
It develops when effective alveolar ventilation becomes inadequate — a sedative-induced fall in minute ventilation can markedly worsen CO₂ retention.
Recall
Gold-standard practical test for hypercapnic failure — and the PaCO₂ cut-off?
tap to flip
Answer
ABG. No universal PaCO₂ cutoff — interpret with pH, chronicity, mental status and work of breathing.
🩺 Think it through
A patient with a COPD exacerbation (or on opioids, or with neuromuscular disease) becomes somnolent. What is happening and what will the ABG show?
Hypercapnic respiratory failure — rising PaCO₂ with respiratory acidosis (the classic setup).
Recall
Preferred ALT ventilatory support in hypercapnic COPD — who qualifies?
tap to flip
Answer
Noninvasive ventilation (NIV) in cooperative COPD patients who can protect the airway. Clue favoring NIV: PaCO₂ >45 mmHg with a suitable acute presentation.
Why it helps: positive-pressure support augments alveolar ventilation and reduces the work of breathing, correcting the acute respiratory acidosis and reducing the need for endotracheal intubation. Invasive ventilation is required if NIV is contraindicated or fails.
Board trap · When NIV is the wrong answerAVOID NIV with severe instability, inability to protect the airway, impaired cooperation/mental status, copious secretions, or major facial injury — these mandate intubation instead.
Recall
Most-tested complication of hypercapnic respiratory failure?
tap to flip
Answer
CO₂ narcosis / respiratory arrest.
  • ★Hypercapnic failure sequence: Treat trigger + ventilatory support → NIV if cooperative, airway-protective COPD patient → NIV failing / arrest / declining consciousness → Intubate.
Board trap · Cardiogenic pulmonary edema vs ARDSCardiogenic edema shows cardiac/volume-overload findings; ARDS requires a nonhydrostatic explanation for the hypoxemia.
Board trap · Pulse oximetry and CO₂Pulse oximetry assesses oxygenation only — it cannot diagnose hypercapnia. Only an ABG measures PaCO₂.

Recall
Classic CAP vignette?
tap to flip
Answer
Acute fever/chills + productive cough + pleuritic pain + crackles/bronchial breath sounds + a new infiltrate.
Recall
Classic organism of CAP?
tap to flip
Answer
Streptococcus pneumoniae.
Recall
First diagnostic test in suspected CAP — and what confirms the pathogen?
tap to flip
Answer
Chest radiograph first. No single universal test establishes both pneumonia and the pathogen — microbiologic isolation confirms etiology when obtained.
Recall
FIRST-LINE (Harrison-era) therapy for uncomplicated outpatient CAP?
tap to flip
Answer
A macrolide or doxycycline.
Recall
CAP with comorbidity (preferred ALT) or inpatient regimen?
tap to flip
Answer
A β-lactam plus macrolide, or a respiratory fluoroquinolone.
Recall
β-lactam monotherapy and the 'atypical' CAP pathogens?
tap to flip
Answer
Atypicals are intrinsically resistant to β-lactams — they lack a peptidoglycan cell wall or otherwise lack the structural target β-lactams need. Use a macrolide, a fluoroquinolone, or a tetracycline.
Recall
Pneumonia clues that point to Legionella pneumophila?
tap to flip
Answer
High fever + gastrointestinal symptoms (diarrhea) + neurologic symptoms (confusion) + hyponatremia; sputum Gram stain with many neutrophils but no visible organisms; poor response to β-lactams.
Recall
Aspiration risk (impaired airway protection) + poor dentition, then a cavitating lesion with pleural effusion → cause?
tap to flip
Answer
Anaerobic infection — may progress to lung abscess and pleural complications such as effusion.
Recall
Severe CAP with hypoxemia / septic shock → ?
tap to flip
Answer
LIFE-SAVING: oxygen/ventilation + prompt effective antibiotics + sepsis resuscitation.
Recall
Most-tested complication of CAP?
tap to flip
Answer
Parapneumonic effusion/empyema or septic shock.
Board trap · CAP not improving by ~72 hoursAVOID simply continuing the same regimen. Reassess the diagnosis, resistance, and complications instead.
🩺 Think it through
A 70-year-old with fever, productive cough and a new infiltrate is confused with a respiratory rate of 32/min. CURB-65 score and disposition?
Score 3 (confusion + RR ≥30 + age ≥65) → ≥3 = severe / ICU consideration.

🦠Viral (Influenza) & Hospital-/Ventilator-Associated Pneumonia12 items▾

Influenza / viral pneumonia vs HAP / VAP
FeatureInfluenza / viral pneumoniaHospital-/ventilator-associated pneumoniaAnswer
Classic vignetteAbrupt fever + headache + severe myalgia + cough in influenza season; severe cases develop dyspnea/hypoxemiaIntubated patient with new/progressive infiltrate + fever/leukocytosis + purulent secretions + worsening oxygenation
Gold-standard testRespiratory RT-PCR (most sensitive/specific)No single perfect test; respiratory cultures improve etiologic specificity
FIRST-LINENeuraminidase inhibitor, commonly oseltamivirBroad empirical antibiotics based on local MDR risk, then de-escalate
AVOIDAspirin in children/adolescents (Reye syndrome)Continuing unnecessarily broad therapy once culture data permit narrowing
  • ✎Uncomplicated influenza regimen: oseltamivir daily for days.
Recall
Hospitalized/complicated influenza presenting beyond the ideal early window — still treat?
tap to flip
Answer
Yes — antiviral therapy should still be given.
  • ✎Rapid influenza antigen tests are fast but only about % sensitive — a negative result does not rule out influenza when suspicion remains high.
Board trap · Positive viral PCR = virus is the only cause?No. Respiratory viruses are detected in healthy adults as well as in pneumonia, so a positive PCR may mean etiologic infection, copathogenicity (viral + bacterial coinfection), colonization, or prolonged shedding after an earlier infection. It does not rule out concurrent bacterial infection — do not withhold or stop antibacterials on the PCR result alone; decide on the overall clinical picture.
Recall
Influenza improves, then fever/cough recur → think?
tap to flip
Answer
Secondary bacterial pneumonia (classic board clue).
Organism to consider especially: Staphylococcus aureus — a recognized post-influenza complication, including severe necrotizing pneumonia from community-associated MRSA.
🧠 Memory toolRelapse vs single illness after influenza
RecursFever/cough return after initial influenza improvement = secondary bacterial pneumonia
SingleOne non-relapsing hypoxemic illness = uncomplicated viral pneumonia → neuraminidase inhibitor
Contrast pair: the second fever is the bacterial one.
Recall
Child or adolescent with influenza — which antipyretic to AVOID and why?
tap to flip
Answer
Aspirin — Reye syndrome.
Recall
Classic VAP pathogens?
tap to flip
Answer
Resistant gram-negatives (including Pseudomonas) and MRSA.
Board trap · Diagnosing VAP on clinical criteria aloneClinical criteria alone may overdiagnose VAP — colonization and noninfectious infiltrates are common.
  • ★Viral pneumonia/ARDS and VAP with shock/respiratory deterioration are LIFE-SAVING situations: oxygen/ventilatory support + sepsis management, adding antibacterial therapy if secondary bacterial pneumonia occurs.
Board trap · VAP with no response in 48–72 hReassess the organism, resistance, diagnosis, and source control.

PTB rapid review
Rapid-review targetBoard answerAnswer
Classic vignetteChronic cough + weight loss + night sweats + low-grade fever ± hemoptysis
Classic radiologic clueUpper-lobe/apical cavitary disease in postprimary TB

Anti-TB drugs — classic toxicities
Anti-TB drugClassic board toxicityAnswer
Isoniazid (INH)Peripheral neuropathy, hepatotoxicity
Rifampin (RIF)Orange body fluids + CYP induction

🧠 Memory toolHRZE — adult daily doses
HIsoniazid (INH) — 5 mg/kg (max 300 mg)
RRifampin (RIF) — 10 mg/kg (max 600 mg)
ZPyrazinamide (PZA) — 25 mg/kg
EEthambutol (EMB) — 15 mg/kg
Doses climb 5 → 10 → 15 → 25 mg/kg: H, R, E, Z.

  • ✎First-line drug-susceptible PTB regimen: months HRZE → months HR.
Recall
Why does pyrazinamide belong to the initial phase of TB therapy?
tap to flip
Answer
PZA is particularly active in acidic environments (inside phagocytes and granulomas, against semi-dormant bacilli) — an early sterilizing effect that permits shortening of standard therapy.
Recall
Role and limitation of the AFB smear?
tap to flip
Answer
Rapid infectiousness clue, but less sensitive than molecular testing/culture.
Transmission is greatest from AFB smear-positive patients, especially those with cavitary pulmonary or laryngeal disease.
Recall
Presumptive TB test in the Philippine setting?
tap to flip
Answer
Xpert MTB/RIF (supplementary point).
Recall
Red-green color discrimination impairment on anti-TB therapy → which drug?
tap to flip
Answer
Ethambutol — optic neuritis.
Action: stop ethambutol promptly when visual acuity or color vision declines and repeat the ocular assessment — early recognition improves the chance of recovery.
Board trap · Monotherapy / incomplete regimen in active TBAVOID active-TB monotherapy or an incomplete regimen — this drives resistance.
Recall
Public-health purpose of directly observed (supervised) TB treatment?
tap to flip
Answer
Improves adherence and treatment completion → fewer treatment failures, relapses and defaults (loss to follow-up), limiting the emergence and spread of drug resistance.
Recall
Massive hemoptysis in PTB → ?
tap to flip
Answer
LIFE-SAVING: secure the airway, then pursue urgent embolization/bronchoscopy/surgery.
Recall
Most-tested complication of PTB?
tap to flip
Answer
Massive hemoptysis or disseminated TB.
Board trap · Positive TST/IGRA = active TB?TST/IGRA indicates TB infection but does not establish active pulmonary TB — do not accept a positive TST/IGRA alone as confirmation.
🩺 Think it through
Chronic cough, weight loss, night sweats and an apical cavity on chest film; the only test back is a positive IGRA. Is active PTB confirmed, and what is the definitive diagnosis?
Not confirmed — IGRA shows infection only. Definitive diagnosis: MTB culture or MTB DNA identification (traditional gold standard: mycobacterial culture).

Older smoker with chronic cough/sputum + progressive exertional dyspnea + prolonged expiration.

Hyperinflation with reduced DLCO.

Does very severe airflow obstruction require extensive emphysema on CT?
tap to flip

No. Advanced COPD often shows extensive emphysema, but a minority with very severe obstruction have virtually no emphysema — small-airways disease can predominate; spirometric severity and CT emphysema burden need not correlate.

FIRST-LINE disease-modifying step in COPD?
tap to flip
Answer
Smoking cessation.
Recall
Why can COPD keep progressing years after the last cigarette?
tap to flip
Answer
In susceptible patients, chronic airway inflammation, protease-mediated tissue injury (protease–antiprotease imbalance) and abnormal repair persist after smoking cessation, continuing structural and functional lung damage.

tap to flip
Answer
Mild intermittent: short-acting bronchodilator.
Persistent: LABA/LAMA.
Recall
Role of ICS in stable COPD?
tap to flip
Answer
Preferred ALT/add-on in selected exacerbation-prone patients, usually combined with a long-acting bronchodilator.
  • ✎Long-term oxygen improves survival at stable PaO₂ ≤ mmHg OR SaO₂ ≤%.
  • ✎Long-term oxygen is also indicated at PaO₂ mmHg or SaO₂ below % with pulmonary hypertension/cor pulmonale.

Most-tested chronic complication of COPD?
tap to flip

Cor pulmonale / chronic respiratory failure.
Board trap · Chronic oral steroids in stable COPDAVOID chronic systemic glucocorticoids in stable COPD. Reserve inhaled steroid combinations for exacerbation-prone phenotypes rather than routine oral steroids. Reason: limited long-term benefit that does not outweigh the substantial risk of systemic adverse effects — an unfavorable benefit–risk profile.

😮‍💨Acute COPD Exacerbation12 items▾

Recall
Classic vignette of an acute COPD exacerbation?
tap to flip
Answer
Known COPD with acutely worsening dyspnea + increased sputum volume and/or purulence.
Recall
Severe COPD exacerbation — what to obtain?
tap to flip
Answer
SpO₂ ± ABG, and a CXR to exclude pneumonia / pneumothorax / CHF.
Recall
FIRST-LINE treatment of a COPD exacerbation?
tap to flip
Answer
Repeated short-acting bronchodilator (SABA) ± ipratropium plus a systemic glucocorticoid.
  • ✎Steroid regimen for a COPD exacerbation: prednisolone mg/day for days.
Recall
When to give antibiotics in a COPD exacerbation?
tap to flip
Answer
Strongly consider when sputum purulence/volume increases or bacterial infection is suspected.

NIV failure, respiratory arrest, altered consciousness, refractory hypoxemia, or progressive hypercapnia.
Recall
Most-tested complication of a COPD exacerbation?
tap to flip

Acute-on-chronic hypercapnic respiratory failure.

🩺 Think it through
A cooperative COPD patient with purulent sputum remains dyspneic after SABA, ipratropium and a systemic steroid; ABG shows PaCO₂ above 45 mmHg and he protects his airway. Next steps?
Antibiotics for the purulent sputum and NIV for the hypercapnia; intubate if NIV fails, he arrests, or consciousness declines.

Recall
Classic vignette of acute severe asthma?

Severe dyspnea + accessory-muscle use + inability to speak normally + low PEF; may progress from loud wheeze to a silent chest.

Clinically plus PEF/FEV₁ when feasible; ABG reserved for severe/deteriorating cases.

A normal or rising PaCO₂ despite severe distress.

Exhaustion, altered consciousness, silent chest, refractory hypoxemia, or rising CO₂ → intubate with a prolonged expiratory time.

Silent chestAirflow too limited to generate wheeze — impending-respiratory-failure emergency, not improvement

An asthmatic in severe distress, initially wheezing loudly, now has a quiet chest and looks exhausted; ABG shows a rising PaCO₂. What does this mean and what is done?
Critical airflow limitation with impending respiratory failure, not improvement → intubate with a prolonged expiratory time.

Shoulder/arm pain and brachial plexus symptoms ± Horner syndrome.

Brain/bone metastases.

tap to flip

An oncogenic driver that predicts sensitivity to EGFR tyrosine-kinase inhibitors — the reason molecular profiling guides targeted therapy.

Board trap · Surgery for SCLC or metastatic NSCLCSCLC is systemic disease → chemotherapy-based treatment even in limited stage; localized NSCLC is potentially surgical. Do not offer curative surgery to SCLC or to metastatic NSCLC. Conversely, medically operable, resectable stage IA NSCLC → surgical resection is the preferred definitive treatment and the best chance of cure — not chemotherapy alone.
Board trap · Same-lobe pneumonia that keeps coming backRecurrent or nonresolving pneumonia in the same region, especially in an older smoker with constitutional symptoms (weight loss), warrants a search for an obstructing lung cancer — cross-sectional imaging and consideration of bronchoscopy — rather than another empiric antibiotic course.
🧠 Memory toolNSCLC vs SCLC — the treatment split
NSCLCAdenocarcinoma / squamous / large-cell — localized disease treated with surgery when operable
SCLCSmall-cell neuroendocrine — treated as systemic disease with chemotherapy ± thoracic radiation even at limited stage

A heavy smoker has a central/hilar mass, bulky mediastinal nodes and hyponatremia; biopsy shows small-cell neuroendocrine carcinoma confined to one hemithorax within a radiation field. Treatment?

🩺 Think it through
An adolescent has progressive pain and swelling near the knee; x-ray shows a destructive metaphyseal lesion with sunburst periosteal reaction and a Codman triangle. What must be done before definitive therapy, and what is the treatment sequence?
Biopsy/histopathology first (planned within sarcoma surgical planning), with MRI for local extent + chest imaging for lung metastasis → neoadjuvant chemotherapy → limb-sparing surgery when feasible → postoperative chemotherapy. Radiotherapy alone is never definitive.

FeatureBoard AnswerAnswer

Recall
Sudden focal deficit → first test, and why?
tap to flip
Answer
Noncontrast CT head — to exclude hemorrhage before reperfusion.
Examination alone cannot reliably tell ischemic from hemorrhagic stroke, so imaging is urgent; reperfusion therapy is used only once hemorrhage is excluded.
Recall
Most sensitive early imaging for infarct?
tap to flip
Answer
Diffusion-weighted MRI.
Recall
Modern definition of TIA?
tap to flip
Answer
Transient ischemic neurologic dysfunction without radiologic infarction; the historical 24-hour boundary is not the key modern concept.

1Pure motor
2Pure sensory
3Ataxic hemiparesis
4Dysarthria-clumsy hand

Recall

tap to flip
Answer
Noncardioembolic → antiplatelet.
Atrial fibrillation → anticoagulation when appropriate.
Symptomatic severe carotid stenosis → may need endarterectomy.

Most-tested complication of acute ischemic stroke?
tap to flip

Cerebral edema / herniation.
Board trap · Normal early CTTempting: "CT is normal, so it is not a stroke." Right: a normal early CT does not exclude ischemic stroke — its urgent role is to exclude hemorrhage, not to confirm infarction.
🩺 Think it through
A patient has sudden painless unilateral weakness and aphasia, last known well within 4.5 h. Noncontrast CT head is normal. What does the CT mean and what is the next move?
The normal CT has done its job — hemorrhage is excluded; it does not rule out infarction. If eligible and BP ≤185/110 mmHg → IV alteplase 0.9 mg/kg (max 90 mg) without unnecessary delay; large-vessel occlusion → mechanical thrombectomy.

What does nimodipine do after aneurysmal SAH?

Improves neurologic outcome.

Classic imaging of an AVM?
tap to flip

Serpiginous vascular nidus with feeding arteries and draining veins.
These abnormal vascular channels may rupture → intracranial hemorrhage.

Board trap · ICH vs SAH vs AVMICH = hypertensive bleed in a deep structure (putamen, thalamus, pons, cerebellum) — AVOID thrombolysis.
Aneurysmal SAH = thunderclap headache from a ruptured berry (saccular) aneurysm, the classic nontraumatic cause of SAH — coiling/clipping + nimodipine.
AVM = young patient with lobar bleed/seizures from a vascular nidus — not every incidental lesion needs treatment.
🩺 Think it through
A patient reports a sudden "worst headache of my life," maximal at onset, with meningismus. Noncontrast CT head is negative. What next?
Lumbar puncture for xanthochromia (appears 6–12 h, persists 1–4 wk) — a negative initial CT does not exclude a compelling SAH presentation.

tap to flip

Convulsion persisting ~≥5 min, or recurrent seizures without regaining baseline consciousness.

tap to flip

🩺 Think it through
A patient is still convulsing more than 5 minutes after onset; EEG is not yet available. What do you do first?
Treat now — IV lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg (do not wait for EEG), check and correct glucose immediately, then add fosphenytoin/phenytoin 20 mg/kg (or valproate/levetiracetam) rather than repeating small benzodiazepine doses.

tap to flip

🧠 Memory toolRabies PEP by vaccination history
0-3-7-14 + 20Never vaccinated: 4 vaccine days + RIG 20 IU/kg
0-3Previously vaccinated: 2 vaccine days, no routine RIG

So absent hydrophobia does not exclude rabies; fever, bladder dysfunction and CSF pleocytosis favor rabies over GBS.

tap to flip

RT-PCR (saliva/CSF/skin/brain), direct fluorescent antibody, rabies-specific antibodies — no single negative test excludes disease.
If clinical suspicion stays high, repeat rabies-specific testing on appropriate specimens.

Treatment once rabies is symptomatic? Outcome?
tap to flip
Answer
No established curative therapy — supportive/palliative care. Symptomatic disease is almost uniformly fatal.
Board trap · Delaying PEP / RIG all IMAVOID waiting for neurologic symptoms before starting indicated PEP; also AVOID injecting all RIG IM without attempting local wound infiltration when feasible.

Board trap · Tetanus vs rabiesTetanus = painful generalized spasms with a clear sensorium — metronidazole + TIG.

Start IV acyclovir 10 mg/kg q8h immediately — do not wait for PCR; continue 21 days if confirmed.

FIRST-LINEMaximal safe resection → radiotherapy + concomitant temozolomide → adjuvant temozolomideObservation (small/asymptomatic); surgical resection (symptomatic/large)Dexamethasone for symptomatic edema
Preferred ALTRecurrence-directed oncologic therapyStereotactic radiosurgery/radiotherapy for selected residual/recurrent/surgically unsuitable diseaseStereotactic radiosurgery for selected limited lesions; surgery for a selected solitary accessible lesion
AVOIDRoutine prophylactic antiseizure medication if the patient has never seizedUnnecessary surgery for every small, stable, incidental lesionAssuming every multiple enhancing lesion is metastatic without considering infection/demyelination in the appropriate host
Most-tested complicationRecurrenceSeizures / recurrence after incomplete resectionSeizures / intracranial mass effect
🧠 Memory toolImaging signature of the three masses
ButterflyGBM — necrotic ring-enhancing mass crossing the corpus callosum
Dural tailMeningioma — dural-based, homogeneously enhancing
Many, gray-whiteMetastases — multiple enhancing lesions with edema at the gray-white junction
Lesion pattern + clinical context: a solitary infiltrative mass favors a primary tumor; multiple lesions, especially with a known cancer, favor metastases.
Recall
Glioblastoma — what class of tumor is it?
tap to flip
Answer
The prototypic high-grade diffuse astrocytic malignancy of adults — a highly aggressive primary brain tumor.
Recall
Brain mass with morning-predominant headache and vomiting → mechanism?
tap to flip
Answer
Raised intracranial pressure from the expanding lesion — headache, vomiting, sometimes papilledema, and impaired consciousness.
Recall
How does a brain tumor cause a new focal seizure in an adult?
tap to flip
Answer
The mass disrupts or infiltrates cortical gray matter, creating an irritable focus of neurons prone to abnormal synchronized firing — so a focal (rather than generalized) seizure is a red flag for a localized structural cause.
Recall
Which primaries classically send metastases to brain? Most common source?
tap to flip
Answer
Lung, breast, melanoma, renal. Lung cancer is the most common source primary.
Recall
Meningioma: observe or operate?
tap to flip
Answer
Observe if small/asymptomatic; surgical resection if symptomatic/large. Stereotactic radiosurgery/radiotherapy for selected residual/recurrent/surgically unsuitable disease.
Recall
Brain metastases: first-line for symptomatic edema, and the focal options?
tap to flip
Answer
Dexamethasone for symptomatic edema.
Stereotactic radiosurgery for selected limited lesions; surgery for a selected solitary accessible lesion.
Recall
Gold-standard test for GBM?
tap to flip
Answer
Contrast-enhanced MRI → tissue histopathology.
  • ✎Symptomatic vasogenic edema from a brain tumor → dexamethasone (GBM dosing mg/day) while definitive therapy is arranged.
  • ✎GBM median survival (Harrison): approximately months even with combined maximal therapy.
  • ★EMERGENCY: herniation or obstructive hydrocephalus from any of the three masses → urgent steroids for vasogenic edema + emergent neurosurgical decompression / CSF diversion.
Board trap · Prophylactic antiseizure drugAVOID routine prophylactic antiseizure medication in a brain-tumor patient who has never seized.
Board trap · "Multiple lesions = metastases"Do not assume every multiple enhancing lesion is metastatic — consider infection/demyelination in the appropriate host. Likewise, not every small, stable, incidental meningioma needs surgery.
Board trap · GBM vs meningioma imagingGBM = infiltrative, necrotic, ring-enhancing intra-axial mass (± butterfly corpus-callosum crossing).
Meningioma = homogeneously enhancing, dural-based extra-axial mass with a dural tail.
Confusing the two changes both prognosis and surgical curability.
Board trap · GBM vs meningioma outcomeGlioblastoma = infiltrative intra-axial necrotic mass, poor prognosis (~14.6–18 months) despite maximal therapy.
Meningioma = extra-axial dural-based mass with a dural tail, often observed or curable with resection.
Recall
Most-tested complication: GBM vs meningioma vs metastases?
tap to flip
Answer
GBM → recurrence.
Meningioma → seizures / recurrence after incomplete resection.
Metastases → seizures / intracranial mass effect.

No imaging; remain active + NSAID or acetaminophen. No red flags = no initial imaging, and bed rest >2 days is avoided.

Low-back pain radiating into one leg with dermatomal numbness ± focal weakness/reflex loss.

L5 — dorsum-of-foot sensory loss, dorsiflexion/great-toe extension weakness, no reflex change. Sensory and myotomal findings localize the root.

Focal disabling: botulinum toxin A first-line.
Generalized: oral baclofen/tizanidine, escalating to intrathecal baclofen if severe and refractory.

A bedbound hemiparetic stroke patient due for gait training has new unilateral leg swelling and acute dyspnea. Continue the session?
No — urgently evaluate for DVT/PE. Continuing rehab through a suspected DVT/PE is an AVOID answer.

⛔Last-Minute "Do NOT Pick This" (All Topics)42 items▾

Board trap · VF/pulseless VTIn VF/pulseless VT, the classic wrong pick is synchronized cardioversion instead of defibrillation.
Right: defibrillate.
Board trap · STEMIIn STEMI, the classic wrong pick is waiting for troponin before reperfusion.
Board trap · NSTEMIIn NSTEMI, the classic wrong pick is fibrinolysis.
Board trap · Infective endocarditis, stableIn Infective endocarditis, stable, the classic wrong pick is antibiotics before obtaining blood cultures.
Board trap · TamponadeIn Tamponade, the classic wrong pick is diuretic alone instead of drainage.
Right: drainage.
Board trap · Symptomatic severe ASIn Symptomatic severe AS, the classic wrong pick is medical therapy as definitive treatment.
Board trap · GI hemorrhagic shockIn GI hemorrhagic shock, the classic wrong pick is endoscopy before adequate stabilization.
Board trap · Acute pancreatitisIn Acute pancreatitis, the classic wrong pick is routine prophylactic antibiotics.
Board trap · CholangitisIn Cholangitis, the classic wrong pick is antibiotics alone despite an obstructed infected biliary system.
Board trap · DKA with K <3.3In DKA with K <3.3, the classic wrong pick is insulin before potassium.
Board trap · PheochromocytomaIn Pheochromocytoma, the classic wrong pick is β-blocker before α-blocker.
Board trap · Hyperkalemia + ECG toxicityIn Hyperkalemia + ECG toxicity, the classic wrong pick is potassium binder alone.
Board trap · PyelonephritisIn Pyelonephritis, the classic wrong pick is nitrofurantoin.
Board trap · Infected obstructing stoneIn Infected obstructing stone, the classic wrong pick is antibiotics alone without drainage.
Board trap · ARDSIn ARDS, the classic wrong pick is high tidal-volume ventilation.
Board trap · Stable COPDIn Stable COPD, the classic wrong pick is chronic systemic glucocorticoids.
Board trap · AsthmaIn Asthma, the classic wrong pick is LABA monotherapy.
Board trap · Severe asthma + rising PaCO₂In Severe asthma + rising PaCO₂, the classic wrong pick is reassurance because CO₂ "normalized".
Board trap · Active TBIn Active TB, the classic wrong pick is monotherapy.
Board trap · Septic arthritisIn Septic arthritis, the classic wrong pick is steroid injection because crystals were found.
Board trap · Early RAIn Early RA, the classic wrong pick is wait for erosions before DMARD.
Board trap · FibromyalgiaIn Fibromyalgia, the classic wrong pick is immunosuppression.
Board trap · Positive ANA aloneIn Positive ANA alone, the classic wrong pick is diagnose SLE.
Board trap · Scleroderma renal crisisIn Scleroderma renal crisis, the classic wrong pick is high-dose steroid instead of ACE inhibitor.
Right: ACE inhibitor.
Board trap · GCA + visual complaintIn GCA + visual complaint, the classic wrong pick is wait for biopsy before steroid.
Board trap · Classic osteosarcoma x-rayIn Classic osteosarcoma x-ray, the classic wrong pick is skip biopsy.
Board trap · Acute ischemic strokeIn Acute ischemic stroke, the classic wrong pick is routine acute heparin.
Board trap · ICHIn ICH, the classic wrong pick is thrombolysis.
Board trap · Status epilepticusIn Status epilepticus, the classic wrong pick is wait for EEG before benzodiazepine.
Board trap · Suspected meningitisIn Suspected meningitis, the classic wrong pick is delay antibiotics for CT/LP.
Board trap · Suspected HSV encephalitisIn Suspected HSV encephalitis, the classic wrong pick is wait for PCR before acyclovir.
Board trap · Rabies exposureIn Rabies exposure, the classic wrong pick is wait for hydrophobia before PEP.
Board trap · Parkinson diseaseIn Parkinson disease, the classic wrong pick is abruptly stop dopaminergic drugs.
Board trap · Alzheimer-type slow declineIn Alzheimer-type slow decline, the classic wrong pick is call acute fluctuating confusion "dementia".
Board trap · Brain tumor without prior seizureIn Brain tumor without prior seizure, the classic wrong pick is routine prophylactic antiseizure medication.
Board trap · Cauda equinaIn Cauda equina, the classic wrong pick is outpatient physical therapy.
Board trap · Post-stroke dysphagiaIn Post-stroke dysphagia, the classic wrong pick is give unrestricted oral liquids.
Board trap · Suspected PE during rehabilitationIn Suspected PE during rehabilitation, the classic wrong pick is continue gait training.
Board trap · Recap rule: DefibrillateShock a pulseless VT/VF; never sync-cardiovert a pulseless rhythm.
Board trap · Recap rule: Drain firstObstructed infection (cholangitis, infected stone, tamponade) always needs source control, not antibiotics/diuretics alone.
Board trap · Recap rule: Stabilize firstResuscitate before scope/EEG/biopsy delays definitive care in a crashing patient.
Board trap · Recap rule: Correct K/Ca before insulin/other drugsHypokalemia and hyperkalemia both demand correction before the "main" therapy proceeds.
